Doeblin Curves

Dongmin Lee    William Lu    Anuran Makur    and Japneet Singh ††thanks: The author ordering is alphabetical. This work was supported by the National Science Foundation (NSF) CAREER Award under Grant CCF-2337808. An earlier version of this paper was presented in part at the 2024 IEEE International Symposium on Information Theory (ISIT) [1].††thanks: Dongmin Lee is with the Department of Computer Science, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN 47907, USA (e-mail: lee4818@purdue.edu).††thanks: William Lu is with the Department of Computer Science, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN 47907, USA (e-mail: lu909@purdue.edu).††thanks: Anuran Makur is with the Department of Computer Science and the Elmore Family School of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN 47907, USA (e-mail: amakur@purdue.edu).††thanks: Japneet Singh is with the Elmore Family School of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN 47907, USA (e-mail: sing1041@purdue.edu).
Abstract

Recent research on Doeblin coefficients has shed light on their usefulness as a multi-way generalization of the Dobrushin contraction coefficient for TV distance, in a separate vein from their classic role in the theory of Markov chain ergodicity. However, strong conditions, such as being bounded away from 00, are typically necessary for Doeblin coefficients to establish the existence of information contraction. Building on recently formulated concepts of nonlinear information contraction, we aim to propose a finer-grained Doeblin-based characterization of multi-way contraction behavior which yields non-vacuous contraction guarantees even for channels whose Doeblin coefficient is 00. To this end, we introduce the notion of a Doeblin curve—a nonlinear function which quantifies the contraction behavior of a Markov kernel on collections of input distributions at specific levels of divergence and power. Through the course of our analysis, we develop a new variational characterization of Doeblin coefficients, present several properties of Doeblin curves, define several versions of power-constrained Doeblin curves, and derive upper and lower bounds using our aforementioned variational characterization. We then utilize these results in diverse areas, including generalization bounds for noisy iterative optimization, error bounds for reliable computation with noisy circuits, and differential privacy guarantees for online iterative algorithms. In particular, we extend results in these areas to broader domains or group settings, leveraging Doeblin curves to reveal finer-grained contraction phenomena than Doeblin coefficients.

Index Terms: 
Doeblin coefficient, Markov kernel, information contraction, reliable computation, generalization error, differential privacy.

I Introduction

Analyzing the contraction properties of channels or Markov kernels is a fundamental problem in information theory stemming back to the celebrated data processing inequality, which states that the ff-divergence between two distributions does not increase after they are passed through a Markov kernel [2, 3]. Data processing inequalities can be strengthened using contraction coefficients [4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9], which quantify the degree to which two distributions contract after being pushed forward through a Markov kernel (also see more recent work [10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18] and the references therein). In some cases, the quantification of this contraction behavior can be extended to an arbitrary collection of distributions represented by another Markov kernel, e.g., using Doeblin coefficients [19].

Historically, such contraction analyses were closely tied to investigating the convergence rate of a Markov chain to its steady-state distribution. Initial work in this vein by Doeblin [20, 21] established exponential convergence rates for all Markov matrices with strictly positive Doeblin coefficients, while more general weak ergodicity results for inhomogeneous Markov chains have been obtained using similar ideas, e.g., [22, Lemma 3]. Furthermore, [19] recently showed that Doeblin coefficients may be perceived as an nn-way generalization of total variation (TV) distance, a view in which the submultiplicativity of Doeblin coefficients corresponds to the data processing inequality for nn input distributions.

However, the utility of Doeblin coefficients remains limited in the regime of channels whose Doeblin coefficient is 00, for which information contraction properties cannot be easily established using existing Doeblin-based techniques. For example, prior work has demonstrated that Markov chains exhibit convergence to stationarity even under much weaker conditions such as drift and local minorization, cf. [23], and a strictly positive Doeblin coefficient may be considered a strong assumption. Consequently, contemporary results in Markov process analysis often shed the dependence on Doeblin coefficients altogether, instead being rooted in alternative methods such as spectral gap (or Poincaré) and logarithmic Sobolev inequalities [24].

The issue of contraction coefficients taking on trivial values exists in broader information-theoretic settings too [25, 14]. For example, Dobrushin’s contraction coefficient for TV distance often takes the value 11 which does not demonstrate any meaningful information contraction [25]. To circumvent this issue, [25] develops nonlinear functions called Dobrushin curves that capture TV contraction even if the contraction coefficient is 11. Propelled by this line of inquiry, we seek to understand Doeblin-based information contraction properties of Markov kernels under general conditions, including the case of zero Doeblin coefficient. To this end, we introduce the notion of a Doeblin curve in this work (also see [1]). This nonlinear function quantifies the degree of contraction exhibited by its associated Markov kernel KK, when applied to an arbitrary collection of input distributions represented by another kernel WW. In contrast to conventional Doeblin coefficients, the nonlinearity of the Doeblin curve captures a more nuanced view of the contraction behavior of KK.

I-A Main Contributions and Outline

We briefly outline the structure of our paper and list our main contributions. Following a discussion of preliminaries, in Section II-A, we present a new variational characterization of Doeblin coefficients as an infimum over arbitrary partitions of the output space. Next, we introduce and formally define the Doeblin curve of a general Markov kernel and enumerate basic properties in Section II-B. We discuss power-constrained versions in Section II-C, derive upper and lower bounds using the aforementioned variational characterization in Section II-D, and present examples of kernels with closed-form Doeblin curves. Notably, in contrast to much of the literature on information contraction and Doeblin coefficients, this work is developed in the context of Markov kernels over general Polish spaces (as opposed to Markov matrices over finite sets).

Building on these theoretical results, we discuss several applications of Doeblin curves in Section III. In Section III-A, we employ Doeblin curves to derive generalization error bounds for noisy iterative algorithms operating on feasible sets with infinite diameter, a situation in which Doeblin coefficients fail to produce non-trivial contraction bounds. In Section III-B, we discuss lower bounds for reliable computation using circuits of noisy qq-ary gates. Lastly, in Section III-C, we utilize our variational characterization of Doeblin coefficients to extend the definition of (ϵ,δ)(\epsilon,\delta)-local differential privacy (LDP) to a group setting, and provide differential privacy guarantees for noisy iterative algorithms in terms of the Doeblin curve of the privacy mechanism.

We provide proofs of our main results in Section IV and proofs for the aforementioned applications in Section V. We defer further technical miscellany to Appendices A, B and C and relate Doeblin curves back to the classic setting of Markov chain ergodicity in Appendix D.

I-B Related Literature

We summarize the prior literature on Doeblin coefficients, multi-way divergence metrics, and strong data processing inequalities (SDPIs). At the outset, Doeblin’s seminal work [20, 21] introduced coupling as a technique for establishing uniform exponential convergence rates of Markov chains with respect to TV distance (also see [26, 27, 28]), and minorization as a technique to prove the weak ergodicity of inhomogeneous Markov chains (also see [22]). Notably, Doeblin coefficients were extremal minorization constants in such techniques. Subsequent results [27, Theorem 3.1], [29, Lemma 5], [30, Section IV-D] established the equivalence between Doeblin minorization and degradation by erasure channels, akin to the view of contraction coefficients for Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence as domination by erasure channels under the less noisy preorder [13]. Doeblin coefficients also find relevance in various machine learning and applied probability problems, such as change detection algorithms [31], regret bounds in multi-armed bandit problems [32], Markov chain Monte Carlo methods [33], analysis of mixing times [34], and estimation of entropy rates [35]. Previous work on strong data processing inequalities [12, Remark 3.2], [36, Section I-D] has also shown how the Doeblin minorization condition yields upper bounds on contraction coefficients for ff-divergences.

Extending the notion of ff-divergence to compare three or more distributions simultaneously is another key avenue of research. For example, [37, 38] develop some general approaches for such extensions. Moreover, [19] established several properties of Doeblin coefficients (including geometric aspects, simultaneous and maximal coupling characterizations, and contraction properties over Bayesian networks), and noted that Doeblin coefficients may be perceived as a multi-way generalization of TV distance. (Interestingly, max-Doeblin coefficients [19], or maximal leakage [39], also share many of these properties [40].)

Much like Doeblin coefficients, the Dobrushin contraction coefficient for TV distance also plays a seminal role in the analysis of Markov kernels. Both the Doeblin and Dobrushin coefficients share key properties such as submultiplicativity [13, 19], and the latter enjoys utility in applications such as generalization error bounds [41], differential privacy guarantees [42], and analysis of reinforcement learning algorithms [43]. As noted earlier, [25] introduced Dobrushin curves to quantify information dissipation in channels with average input cost constraint even when their Dobrushin coefficient is trivially 11. Akin to this nonlinear perspective, other studies [13, 14] developed strong data processing inequalities which capture similar fine-grained contraction behavior. In this paper, we extend these ideas to the realm of Doeblin coefficients, demonstrating that analogous nonlinear enhancements can be devised to broaden the efficacy of Doeblin-based approaches for characterizing contraction behavior in general settings.

II Main Results on Doeblin Curves

We begin by recalling the maximal coupling characterization of Doeblin coefficients [19, Theorem 2] (also see [47]) defined as follows. Consider a collection of probability measures {Pi}i∈ℐ\{P_{i}\}_{i\in\mathcal{I}} where ℐ\mathcal{I} is a Polish index set and each probability measure PiP_{i} is on a respective Polish space (𝒴i,ℱ𝒴i)(\mathcal{Y}_{i},\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}_{i}}). A ​c​o​u​p​l​i​n​g\emph{coupling} of probability measures {Pi}i∈ℐ\{P_{i}\}_{i\in\mathcal{I}} is a collection {Yi}i∈ℐ\{Y_{i}\}_{i\in\mathcal{I}} of random variables all defined on the common measure space ⊗i∈ℐ(𝒴i,ℱ𝒴i)\otimes_{i\in\mathcal{I}}(\mathcal{Y}_{i},\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}_{i}}), equipped with a (joint) probability measure ℙ\mathbb{P} such that for all i∈ℐi\in\mathcal{I}, the marginal probability law of YiY_{i} on (𝒴i,ℱ𝒴i)(\mathcal{Y}_{i},\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}_{i}}) is equal to PiP_{i}. (Since each (𝒴i,ℱ𝒴i)(\mathcal{Y}_{i},\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}_{i}}) is Polish, results such as the Kolmogorov extension theorem guarantee the existence of measures ℙ\mathbb{P} on the infinite collection of random variables {Yi}i∈ℐ\{Y_{i}\}_{i\in\mathcal{I}} which are consistent with finite dimensional distributions [49].) With this groundwork established, the following proposition states the desired maximal coupling characterization for Polish spaces.

Proposition 1 (Maximal Coupling Characterization of Doeblin Coefficients).

Let K:𝒳×ℱ𝒴→[0,1]K\colon\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}}\rightarrow[0,1] be a Markov kernel defined over Polish spaces (𝒳,ℱ𝒳)(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{X}}) and (𝒴,ℱ𝒴)(\mathcal{Y},\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}}). Then,

τ(K)=supℙ:Yx∼K(⋅∣x)ℙ(∀x,x′∈𝒳,Yx=Yx′),\tau(K)=\sup_{\mathbb{P}:Y_{x}\sim K(\cdot\mid x)}\mathbb{P}\left(\forall x,x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X},\,Y_{x}=Y_{x^{\prime}}\right), (13)

where the supremum is taken over all couplings {Yx}x∈𝒳\{Y_{x}\}_{x\in\mathcal{X}} of the probability measures {K(⋅∣x)}x∈𝒳\{K({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid x)\}_{x\in\mathcal{X}}.

Proposition 1 is proved in Section IV-A for completeness. We remark that for any Markov kernel KK, the supremum in Equation 13 is achieved by the construction in Equation 68, which we refer to as the “maximal coupling” for the remainder of this paper. Next, we present our main results, beginning with a new variational characterization of Doeblin coefficients.

II-A Variational Characterization of Doeblin Coefficients

Our first main result is a new variational characterization of Doeblin coefficients, expressed as an infimum over arbitrary partitions of the underlying space. In this sense, our result is comparable to the Gel’fand-Yaglom-Peres variational characterization of KL divergence [50] or the extensions to ff-divergences in [51], [46, Theorem 7.6].

Theorem 1 (Variational Characterization of Doeblin Coefficient).

Let K:𝒳×ℱ𝒴→[0,1]K\colon\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}}\rightarrow[0,1] be an absolutely continuous Markov kernel defined over Polish spaces (𝒳,ℱ𝒳)(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{X}}) and (𝒴,ℱ𝒴)(\mathcal{Y},\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}}). Then,

τ⁡(K)=infn∈ℕinfx1,…,xn∈𝒳infn-partition of 𝒴A1,…,An∑i=1nK⁡(Ai∣xi),\tau(K)=\inf_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\inf_{x_{1},\dots,x_{n}\in\mathcal{X}}\inf_{\begin{subarray}{c}\text{$n$-partition of $\mathcal{Y}$}\\ A_{1},\dots,A_{n}\end{subarray}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}K(A_{i}\mid x_{i}), (14)

where the innermost infimum is taken with respect to all measurable nn-partitions A1,...,An∈ℱ𝒴A_{1},\mathinner{\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp},A_{n}\in\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}}, i.e., Ai∩Aj=∅A_{i}\cap A_{j}=\varnothing for all i≠ji\neq j and ⋃i=1nAi=𝒴\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}=\mathcal{Y}.

Theorem 1 is proved in Section IV-A. The proof uses the characterization of Doeblin coefficients in Equation 11 and the Radon-Nikodym theorem to express τ⁡(K)\tau(K) in terms of the density of the greatest common component of KK. To relate this quantity to the individual densities d​K⁡d​μ(⋅∣x)\frac{\mathrm{d}K}{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu}({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid x) for x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}, we utilize the notion of lattice infimum as a measurable analogue of pointwise infimum, so that the lattice infimum of uncountably many measurable functions d​Kd​μ(⋅∣x)\frac{\mathrm{d}K}{\mathrm{d}\mu}({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid x) (indexed by x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}) remains measurable. Approximating this uncountable lattice infimum with a countable sequence gives rise to the infima over n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} and x1,...,xn∈𝒳x_{1},\mathinner{\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp},x_{n}\in\mathcal{X} in Theorem 1, and we complete the proof by leveraging the following proposition to convert the integral of the pointwise minimum of finitely many densities into an infimum over partitions.

Proposition 2 (Integral Characterization of Infimum).

Let K:𝒳×ℱ𝒴→[0,1]K\colon\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}}\rightarrow[0,1] be an absolutely continuous Markov kernel defined over Polish spaces (𝒳,ℱ𝒳)(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{X}}) and (𝒴,ℱ𝒴)(\mathcal{Y},\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}}). For any fixed x1,...,xn∈𝒳x_{1},\mathinner{\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp},x_{n}\in\mathcal{X} and any fixed constants γ1,...,γn≥0\gamma_{1},\mathinner{\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp},\gamma_{n}\geq 0, we have

infn-partition of 𝒴A1,…,An∑i=1nγiK(Ai∣xi)=∫𝒴(mini∈[n]γi⁡d​K⁡d​μ(⋅∣xi))dμ.\inf_{\begin{subarray}{c}\text{$n$-partition of $\mathcal{Y}$}\\ A_{1},\dots,A_{n}\end{subarray}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\gamma_{i}K(A_{i}\mid x_{i})=\int_{\mathcal{Y}}\left(\min_{i\in[n]}\gamma_{i}\frac{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}K}{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu}({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid x_{i})\right)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu. (15)

Proposition 2 is proved in Section IV-A and is also used in the proofs of subsequent results. We remark that Proposition 2 may be interpreted as a special case of Theorem 1 where 𝒳\mathcal{X} is finite. To see this, observe that whereas the infima over n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} and x1,...,xn∈𝒳x_{1},\mathinner{\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp},x_{n}\in\mathcal{X} in Theorem 1 define the finite subset of 𝒳\mathcal{X} included in the sum (and thus the infinite subset of 𝒳\mathcal{X} omitted from the sum), they are unnecessary when 𝒳\mathcal{X} is finite, as any xi∈𝒳x_{i}\in\mathcal{X} may be “omitted” from the sum by simply taking the respective AiA_{i} to be ∅\emptyset. We note that by imposing stronger regularity conditions on KK, we may prove Theorem 1 without the use of lattice infima; we refer interested readers to Appendix B for an analytically simpler argument under equicontinuity assumptions on d​Kd​μ\frac{\mathrm{d}K}{\mathrm{d}\mu}.

Throughout the rest of the paper, we find it helpful to define a notion of constrained Doeblin coefficient33 3 The constrained Doeblin coefficient τ𝒮​(K)\tau_{\mathcal{S}}(K) is essentially the (unconstrained) Doeblin coefficient τ⁡(K′)\tau(K^{\prime}) of the kernel K′K^{\prime} obtained by restricting the input space of KK to 𝒮\mathcal{S}. Hence, Theorem 1 also holds for constrained Doeblin coefficients by taking the middle infimum over x1,...,xn∈𝒮x_{1},\mathinner{\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp},x_{n}\in\mathcal{S} instead of 𝒳\mathcal{X}. for a Markov kernel K:𝒳×ℱ𝒴→[0,1]K\colon\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}}\rightarrow[0,1] and a measurable set 𝒮∈ℱ𝒳\mathcal{S}\in\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{X}} as

τ𝒮​(K)\displaystyle\tau_{\mathcal{S}}(K) ≜sup{α∈ℝ:∃π∈𝒫,∀x∈𝒮,K(⋅∣x)≥απ},\displaystyle\triangleq\sup\bigl\{\alpha\in\mathbb{R}:\exists\pi\in\mathscr{P},\,\forall x\in\mathcal{S},\,K({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid x)\geq\alpha\pi\bigr\}, (16)
ρ𝒮​(K)\displaystyle\rho_{\mathcal{S}}(K) ≜1−τ𝒮​(K).\displaystyle\triangleq 1-\tau_{\mathcal{S}}(K). (17)

We remark that ρ𝒮​(K)\rho_{\mathcal{S}}(K) is monotonically non-decreasing in 𝒮\mathcal{S}, i.e., for any two sets ℛ,𝒮∈ℱ𝒳\mathcal{R},\mathcal{S}\in\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{X}} such that ℛ⊆𝒮\mathcal{R}\subseteq\mathcal{S}, we have ρℛ​(K)≤ρ𝒮​(K)\rho_{\mathcal{R}}(K)\leq\rho_{\mathcal{S}}(K).

II-B Doeblin Curves

As our centerpiece contribution, we introduce the notion of a Doeblin curve to capture contraction properties of Markov kernels whose Doeblin coefficient is 00. For any Polish space (𝒰,ℱ𝒰)(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{U}}), define the composition of two kernels W:𝒰×ℱ𝒳→ℝ+W\colon\mathcal{U}\times\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{X}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{+} and K:𝒳×ℱ𝒴→ℝ+K\colon\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{+} as the kernel W​K:𝒰×ℱ𝒴→ℝ+WK\colon\mathcal{U}\times\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{+} given by

∀u∈𝒰,∀A∈ℱ𝒴,W​K​(A∣u)≜∫𝒳K⁡(A∣x)​W​(⁡𝑑x∣u).\forall u\in\mathcal{U},\,\forall A\in\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}},\quad WK(A\mid u)\triangleq\!\int_{\mathcal{X}}\!K(A\mid x)\,W(\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x\mid u). (18)

Now, we define the Doeblin curve of a Markov kernel K:𝒳×ℱ𝒴→[0,1]K\colon\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}}\rightarrow[0,1] as the function FK​(⋅,𝒢):[0,1]→[0,1]\mathrm{F}_{K}({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot\mkern 2.0mu};\mathcal{G})\colon[0,1]\rightarrow[0,1] given by

FK(t;𝒢)≜sup{ρ(WK):ρ(W)≤t,W∈𝒢},\displaystyle\mathrm{F}_{K}(t;\mathcal{G})\triangleq\sup\left\{\rho(WK):\rho(W)\leq t,\,W\in\mathcal{G}\right\}, (19)

where the supremum is taken over all Markov kernels W:𝒰×ℱ𝒳→[0,1]W\colon\mathcal{U}\times\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{X}}\rightarrow[0,1] from all Polish spaces (𝒰,ℱ𝒰)(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{U}}), such that WW belongs to some non-empty constraint set 𝒢\mathcal{G}. We remark that Doeblin curves generalize the notion of Dobrushin curves in [25], just as Doeblin coefficients generalize contraction coefficients for TV distance. When 𝒢\mathcal{G} only contains Markov kernels W:𝒰×ℱ𝒳→[0,1]W:\mathcal{U}\times\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{X}}\rightarrow[0,1] where |𝒰|=2|\mathcal{U}|=2, the Doeblin curve FK​(⋅,𝒢)\mathrm{F}_{K}({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot\mkern 2.0mu};\mathcal{G}) reduces to the Dobrushin curve of KK, F𝖳𝖵(t)≜sup{∥K(⋅∣P)−K(⋅∣Q)∥𝖳𝖵:∥P−Q∥𝖳𝖵≤t,(P,Q)∈𝒢}F_{\mathsf{TV}}(t)\triangleq\sup\{\lVert K({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid P)-K({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid Q)\rVert_{\mathsf{TV}}:\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathsf{TV}}\leq t,(P,Q)\in\mathcal{G}\} [25, Equation (32)] (note that a Markov kernel W:𝒰×ℱ𝒳→[0,1]W\colon\mathcal{U}\times\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{X}}\rightarrow[0,1] is an UU-indexed family of probability distributions with cardinality |𝒰||\mathcal{U}|, thus a pair of probability distributions (P,Q)(P,Q) each supported on 𝒳\mathcal{X} is equivalent to a binary-source Markov kernel W:{0,1}×ℱ𝒳→[0,1]W:\{0,1\}\times\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{X}}\to[0,1] with ρ⁡(W)=∥P−Q∥𝖳𝖵\rho(W)=\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathsf{TV}}).

We define the joint range of the input and output complementary Doeblin coefficients as 𝔉⁡(K,𝒢)≜cl{(ρ⁡(W),ρ⁡(W​K)):W∈𝒢}⊆[0,1]2\mathfrak{F}(K;\mathcal{G})\triangleq\cl\{(\rho(W),\rho(WK)):\allowbreak W\in\mathcal{G}\}\subseteq[0,1]^{2}, where cl\cl denotes closure. Specifically, the joint range 𝔉⁡(K,𝒢)\mathfrak{F}(K;\mathcal{G}) is contained within the set {(t,y)∈[0,1]2:y≤FK​(t,𝒢)}\{(t,y)\in[0,1]^{2}:y\leq\mathrm{F}_{K}(t;\mathcal{G})\}. For any kernel KK, the Doeblin curve FK​(t,𝒢)\mathrm{F}_{K}(t;\mathcal{G}) is monotonically non-decreasing in tt for any fixed constraint set 𝒢\mathcal{G}. Also, the Doeblin curve FK​(t,𝒢)\mathrm{F}_{K}(t;\mathcal{G}) and joint range 𝔉⁡(K,𝒢)\mathfrak{F}(K;\mathcal{G}) are monotonically non-decreasing in 𝒢\mathcal{G}, i.e., for any two sets of kernels 𝒢,ℋ\mathcal{G},\mathcal{H} such that 𝒢⊆ℋ\mathcal{G}\subseteq\mathcal{H}, we have FK​(⋅,𝒢)≤FK​(⋅,ℋ)\mathrm{F}_{K}({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot\mkern 2.0mu};\mathcal{G})\leq\mathrm{F}_{K}({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot\mkern 2.0mu};\mathcal{H}) and 𝔉⁡(K,𝒢)⊆𝔉⁡(K,ℋ)\mathfrak{F}(K;\mathcal{G})\subseteq\mathfrak{F}(K;\mathcal{H}).

By submultiplicativity of complementary Doeblin coefficients [22, Section 4], [19, Theorem 1], we have ρ⁡(W​K)≤ρ⁡(W)​ρ​(K)\rho(WK)\leq\rho(W)\rho(K). Hence, the Doeblin curve and joint range satisfy the outer bounds

FK​(t,𝒢)\displaystyle\mathrm{F}_{K}(t;\mathcal{G}) ≤ρ⁡(K)​t,\displaystyle\leq\rho(K)\,t, (20)
𝔉⁡(K,𝒢)\displaystyle\mathfrak{F}(K;\mathcal{G}) ⊆{(t,y)∈[0,1]2:y≤ρ⁡(K)​t},\displaystyle\subseteq\{(t,y)\in[0,1]^{2}:y\leq\rho(K)\,t\}, (21)

and since ρ⁡(K)≤1\rho(K)\leq 1, we have

FK​(t,𝒢)≤t,𝔉⁡(K,𝒢)⊆{(t,y)∈[0,1]2:y≤t}.\mathrm{F}_{K}(t;\mathcal{G})\leq t,\quad\mathfrak{F}(K;\mathcal{G})\subseteq\{(t,y)\in[0,1]^{2}:y\leq t\}. (22)

Figure 1 presents the numerically simulated joint range for a discrete memoryless channel 𝐊∈ℝ𝗌𝗍𝗈5×5\mathbf{K}\in\mathbb{R}_{\mathsf{sto}}^{5\times 5}, comprising 1 million instances of 𝐖\mathbf{W} sampled uniformly from the set of 5×55\times 5 row stochastic matrices. The blue dashed line depicts the Doeblin curve of 𝐊\mathbf{K} obtained analytically from Proposition 3, Part 2. The blue dots represent numerically sampled points (ρ⁡(𝐖),ρ⁡(𝐖𝐊))∈𝔉⁡(𝐊,ℝ𝗌𝗍𝗈5×5)(\rho(\mathbf{W}),\rho(\mathbf{W}\mathbf{K}))\in\mathfrak{F}(\mathbf{K};\mathbb{R}_{\mathsf{sto}}^{5\times 5}) in the joint range of 𝐊\mathbf{K}. The figure shows that when 𝐖\mathbf{W} is uniformly sampled, such as in settings where channel inputs do not inherently tend towards degenerate regions of the probability simplex, the corresponding points in the joint range indicate noticeably more information contraction than the worst-case bound given by the Doeblin curve would suggest.

We enumerate several additional properties of Doeblin curves in the following proposition.44 4 This proposition supersedes [1, Proposition 3]. For brevity, we call a Markov kernel W:𝒰×ℱ𝒳→[0,1]W\colon\mathcal{U}\times\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{X}}\rightarrow[0,1] a constant kernel if there exists a fixed probability measure π:ℱ𝒳→[0,1]\pi\colon\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{X}}\rightarrow[0,1] such that W(⋅∣u)=π(⋅)W({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid u)=\pi({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot\mkern 2.0mu}) for all u∈𝒰u\in\mathcal{U}.

Proposition 3 (Properties of Doeblin Curves).

The Doeblin curve defined in Equation 19 satisfies the following properties:

  1. 1.

    (Data processing property) Given Markov kernels K1K_{1} and K2K_{2} and constraint sets 𝒢1\mathcal{G}_{1} and 𝒢2\mathcal{G}_{2}, the Doeblin curve of the composite channel represented by the diagram 𝒳1​⟶K1​𝒴1=𝒳2​⟶K2​𝒴2\mathcal{X}_{1}\overset{K_{1}}{\longrightarrow}\mathcal{Y}_{1}=\mathcal{X}_{2}\overset{K_{2}}{\longrightarrow}\mathcal{Y}_{2}\,, with constraint set 𝒢\mathcal{G} consisting of all kernels WW such that W∈𝒢1W\in\mathcal{G}_{1} and W​K1∈𝒢2WK_{1}\in\mathcal{G}_{2}, satisfies FK1​K2​(t,𝒢)≤FK2​(FK1​(t,𝒢1),𝒢2)\mathrm{F}_{K_{1}K_{2}}(t;\mathcal{G})\leq\mathrm{F}_{K_{2}}\left(\mathrm{F}_{K_{1}}\left(t;\mathcal{G}_{1}\right);\mathcal{G}_{2}\right).

  2. 2.

    (Sharpness) For any Markov kernel K:𝒳×ℱ𝒴→[0,1]K\colon\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}}\rightarrow[0,1] and any convex constraint set 𝒢\mathcal{G} containing the identity kernel Ξ:𝒳×ℱ𝒳→[0,1]\Xi\colon\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{X}}\rightarrow[0,1] from 𝒳\mathcal{X} to 𝒳\mathcal{X}, i.e., Ξ(⋅∣u)=δu(⋅)\Xi({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid u)=\updelta_{u}({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot\mkern 2.0mu}) for all u∈𝒳u\in\mathcal{X}, and a constant kernel W¯:𝒳×ℱ𝒳→[0,1]\bar{W}\colon\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{X}}\rightarrow[0,1], i.e., W¯(⋅∣u)=π(⋅)\bar{W}({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid u)=\pi({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot\mkern 2.0mu}) for all u∈𝒳u\in\mathcal{X} for some fixed probability measure π:ℱ𝒳→[0,1]\pi\colon\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{X}}\rightarrow[0,1], the Doeblin curve FK​(t,𝒢)\mathrm{F}_{K}(t;\mathcal{G}) achieves the bound in Equation 21 with equality, i.e., FK​(t,𝒢)=ρ⁡(K)​t\mathrm{F}_{K}(t;\mathcal{G})=\rho(K)\,t.

  3. 3.

    (Super-homogeneity) For any Markov kernel K:𝒳×ℱ𝒴→[0,1]K\colon\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}}\rightarrow[0,1] and any convex constraint set 𝒢\mathcal{G} containing a constant kernel W¯:𝒰×ℱ𝒳→[0,1]\bar{W}\colon\mathcal{U}\times\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{X}}\rightarrow[0,1], the Doeblin curve FK​(t,𝒢)\mathrm{F}_{K}(t;\mathcal{G}) satisfies FK​(λ​t,𝒢)≥λ​FK​(t,𝒢)\mathrm{F}_{K}(\lambda t;\mathcal{G})\geq\lambda\mathrm{F}_{K}(t;\mathcal{G}) for all λ∈[0,1]\lambda\in[0,1] and t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1], or equivalently, the function t↦FK​(t,𝒢)/tt\mapsto\mathrm{F}_{K}(t;\mathcal{G})/t is non-increasing.

  4. 4.

    (Lipschitz continuity) For any Markov kernel K:𝒳×ℱ𝒴→[0,1]K\colon\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}}\rightarrow[0,1] and any convex constraint set 𝒢\mathcal{G} containing a constant kernel W¯:𝒰×ℱ𝒳→[0,1]\bar{W}\colon\mathcal{U}\times\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{X}}\rightarrow[0,1], the Doeblin curve FK​(t,𝒢)\mathrm{F}_{K}(t;\mathcal{G}) is 11-Lipschitz continuous in tt.

Proposition 3 is proved in Section IV-B, primarily by using the fact that convex combinations of any Markov kernel with a constant kernel linearly interpolate ρ\rho. We emphasize that the super-homogeneity property (Proposition 3, Part 3) does not necessarily imply that FK\mathrm{F}_{K} is concave, and the concavity of FK\mathrm{F}_{K} is also unknown in the Dobrushin case [25, Remark 1].

Although the joint range 𝔉⁡(K,𝒢)\mathfrak{F}(K;\mathcal{G}) is contained within the area under the Doeblin curve FK​(⋅,𝒢)\mathrm{F}_{K}({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot\mkern 2.0mu};\mathcal{G}) due to the definition of FK\mathrm{F}_{K} as a supremum, it is not necessarily the entire area under FK\mathrm{F}_{K}, as shown by the following counterexample.

Proposition 4 (Joint Range of 2×n2\times n Discrete Channels).

The joint range of any discrete memoryless channel 𝐊∈ℝ𝗌𝗍𝗈2×n\mathbf{K}\in\mathbb{R}_{\mathsf{sto}}^{2\times n}, considering inputs 𝐖∈ℝ𝗌𝗍𝗈m×2\mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{R}_{\mathsf{sto}}^{m\times 2} with any number of rows m≥2m\geq 2, is the line 𝔉⁡(𝐊,⋃m≥2ℝ𝗌𝗍𝗈m×2)={(t,ρ⁡(𝐊)​t):t∈[0,1]}\mathfrak{F}\bigl(\mathbf{K};\bigcup_{m\geq 2}\mathbb{R}_{\mathsf{sto}}^{m\times 2}\bigr)=\left\{(t,\rho(\mathbf{K})\,t):t\in[0,1]\right\}.

Proposition 4 is proved in Section IV-B.

II-C Power-Constrained Doeblin Curves

Inspired by earlier developments of nonlinear information contraction [25], we note that the amount by which input distributions contract after passing through a channel depends on the power level of the input distributions. Hence, power constraints on the input kernel WW admit natural and useful classes of constraint sets 𝒢\mathcal{G} which we consider in our subsequent analysis. While [25] (which only considers the |𝒰|=2|\mathcal{U}|=2 case) uses the average power |||W|||𝖠≜𝔼⁡[∫𝒳M⁡(‖x‖)​W​(𝑑x∣U)]|\mathchoice{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-2.5mu}{}\mathinner{|\mathchoice{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-2.5mu}{}\mathinner{|W|}\mathchoice{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-2.5mu}{}|}\mathchoice{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-2.5mu}{}|_{\mathsf{A}}\triangleq\mathbb{E}\left[\int_{\mathcal{X}}M(\left\lVert x\right\rVert)\,W(\mathrm{d}x\mid U)\right] (where the expectation is taken over U∼𝖡𝖾𝗋𝗇𝗈𝗎𝗅𝗅𝗂⁡(1/2)U\sim\mathsf{Bernoulli}(1/2)) to measure the power level of a kernel W:{0,1}×ℱ𝒳→[0,1]W\colon\{0,1\}\times\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{X}}\to[0,1], this definition implicitly assumes the marginal distribution of UU and thus does not generalize to kernels with arbitrary 𝒰\mathcal{U} (especially when 𝒰\mathcal{U} is not compact, e.g., when 𝒰=ℝ\mathcal{U}=\mathbb{R}). Instead, we define two notions of power that extremize over 𝒰\mathcal{U} to avoid depending on the marginal distribution of UU.

Definition 1 (Power Level).

Let (𝒳,∥⋅∥)(\mathcal{X},\lVert{\mkern 2.0mu\cdot\mkern 2.0mu}\rVert) be a separable Banach space equipped with the Borel σ\sigma-algebra ℱ𝒳\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{X}} induced by the norm topology. Given some convex and strictly increasing power function M:ℝ+→ℝ+M\colon\mathbb{R}_{+}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{+} with M⁡(0)=0M(0)=0, we define the following notions of power level for a Markov kernel W:𝒰×ℱ𝒳→[0,1]W\colon\mathcal{U}\times\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{X}}\rightarrow[0,1].

  • •

    Uniform average power:

    ‖|W|‖𝖴𝖠≜supu∈𝒰∫𝒳M⁡(‖x‖)​W​(⁡𝑑x∣u).\left|\mathchoice{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-2.5mu}{}\left|\mathchoice{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-2.5mu}{}\left|W\right|\mathchoice{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-2.5mu}{}\right|\mathchoice{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-2.5mu}{}\right|_{\mathsf{UA}}\triangleq\sup_{u\in\mathcal{U}}\int_{\mathcal{X}}M(\left\lVert x\right\rVert)\,W(\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x\mid u). (23)
  • •

    Average extremal power: Let ℙ\mathbb{P} be the maximal coupling of random variables {Xu}u∈𝒰\{X_{u}\}_{u\in\mathcal{U}} with Xu∼W(⋅∣u)X_{u}\sim W({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid u) for each u∈𝒰u\in\mathcal{U}, as defined in Equation 68. Then,

    ‖|W|‖𝖠𝖤≜𝔼⁡[supu∈𝒰M⁡(‖Xu‖)],\left|\mathchoice{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-2.5mu}{}\left|\mathchoice{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-2.5mu}{}\left|W\right|\mathchoice{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-2.5mu}{}\right|\mathchoice{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-2.5mu}{}\right|_{\mathsf{AE}}\triangleq\mathbb{E}\left[\sup_{u\in\mathcal{U}}M(\left\lVert X_{u}\right\rVert)\right], (24)

    where the expectation is taken with respect to the maximal coupling {Xu}u∈𝒰∼ℙ\{X_{u}\}_{u\in\mathcal{U}}\sim\mathbb{P}, and we only define this notion of power for kernels WW such that supu∈𝒰M⁡(∥Xu∥)\sup_{u\in\mathcal{U}}M(\lVert X_{u}\rVert) is measurable.

The uniform average power and average extremal power have several desirable properties. Furthermore, we note that each of the power-constrained Doeblin curves satisfies the following homogeneity property (akin to Dobrushin curves).

Proposition 5 (Homogeneity of Power-Constrained Doeblin Curves).

For any Markov kernel K:𝒳×ℱ𝒴→[0,1]K\colon\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}}\rightarrow[0,1], the power-constrained Doeblin curves FK𝖴𝖠\mathrm{F}_{K}^{\mathsf{UA}} and FK𝖠𝖤\mathrm{F}_{K}^{\mathsf{AE}} satisfy FK𝖴𝖠​(λ​t,λ​p)=λ​FK𝖴𝖠​(t,p)\mathrm{F}_{K}^{\mathsf{UA}}(\lambda t;\lambda p)=\lambda\mathrm{F}_{K}^{\mathsf{UA}}(t;p) and FK𝖠𝖤​(λ​t,λ​p)=λ​FK𝖠𝖤​(t,p)\mathrm{F}_{K}^{\mathsf{AE}}(\lambda t;\lambda p)=\lambda\mathrm{F}_{K}^{\mathsf{AE}}(t;p) for all λ∈ℝ+\lambda\in\mathbb{R}_{+} such that λ​t≤1\lambda t\leq 1.

Proposition 5 is proved in Section IV-B using similar arguments based on convex combinations with constant kernels as those used in the proof of Proposition 3. In addition, the Doeblin curves of certain classes of kernels such as additive noise channels are invariant under scaling (when the power constraint is scaled accordingly) as the following proposition shows.

Proposition 6 (Scale Invariance of Power-Constrained Doeblin Curves for Additive Noise Channels).

Let 𝒳=𝒴=ℝd\mathcal{X}=\mathcal{Y}=\mathbb{R}^{d}. Suppose Kσ:𝒳×ℱ𝒴→[0,1]K_{\sigma}\colon\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}}\to[0,1] is an additive noise channel parameterized by σ\sigma such that

Kσ​(A∣𝐱)=∫A1σd​f​(𝐲−𝐱σ)​⁡𝑑𝐲K_{\sigma}(A\mid\mathbf{x})=\int_{A}\frac{1}{\sigma^{d}}f\left(\frac{\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x}}{\sigma}\right)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mathbf{y} (25)

where f:ℝd→ℝ+f\colon\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}_{+} is a probability density function. Then, if the power function is M⁡(z)=z2M(z)=z^{2}, FKσ𝖴𝖠​(t,p)=FK1𝖴𝖠​(t,p/σ2)\mathrm{F}_{K_{\sigma}}^{\mathsf{UA}}(t;p)=\mathrm{F}_{K_{1}}^{\mathsf{UA}}(t;p/\sigma^{2}) for all σ>0\sigma>0 and p≥0p\geq 0.

Proposition 6 is proved in Section IV-B.

II-D Bounds on Power-Constrained Doeblin Curves

In this subsection, we present upper and lower bounds on the power-constrained Doeblin curves for a general kernel and provide examples of kernels whose Doeblin curves may be computed in closed form. Throughout this analysis, let (𝒳,∥⋅∥)(\mathcal{X},\lVert{\mkern 2.0mu\cdot\mkern 2.0mu}\rVert) be a separable Banach space equipped with the Borel σ\sigma-algebra ℱ𝒳\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{X}} induced by the norm topology, let (𝒴,ℱ𝒴)(\mathcal{Y},\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}}) be an arbitrary Polish space, and let K:𝒳×ℱ𝒴→[0,1]K\colon\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}}\rightarrow[0,1] be an absolutely continuous Markov kernel. Let ℬ⁡(a,r)⊂𝒳\mathcal{B}(a,r)\subset\mathcal{X} denote the closed ball centered at a∈𝒳a\in\mathcal{X} with radius rr in the ∥⋅∥\|{\mkern 2.0mu\cdot\mkern 2.0mu}\|-norm. Define functions θ:𝒳×ℝ+→[0,1]\theta\colon\mathcal{X}\times\mathbb{R}_{+}\rightarrow[0,1] and Θ:ℝ+→[0,1]\Theta\colon\mathbb{R}_{+}\rightarrow[0,1] as

θ⁡(a,r)≜ρℬ⁡(a,r)​(K),Θ⁡(r)≜supa∈𝒳θ⁡(a,r).\theta(a,r)\triangleq\rho_{\mathcal{B}(a,r)}(K),\quad\Theta(r)\triangleq\sup_{a\in\mathcal{X}}\theta(a,r). (26)

We remark that Θ\Theta (and hence the upper concave envelope Θinvbreve\invbreve{\Theta}, by Lemma 9, Part 2) are non-decreasing, because ρ𝒮\rho_{\mathcal{S}} is non-decreasing in 𝒮\mathcal{S} as previously mentioned. Since 𝒳\mathcal{X} is a Banach space, there exists an element 𝟎∈𝒳\mathbf{0}\in\mathcal{X} such that ∥𝟎∥=0\lVert\mathbf{0}\rVert=0; we denote this element in bold font to distinguish it from the scalar 0∈ℝ0\in\mathbb{R}. Let

γ≜sup{rad(𝒮)⦀𝒮⦀∞:𝒮⊂𝒳, 0<|||𝒮|||∞<∞}\gamma\triangleq\sup\left\{\frac{\rad(\mathcal{S})}{\left|\mathchoice{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-2.5mu}{}\left|\mathchoice{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-2.5mu}{}\left|\mathcal{S}\right|\mathchoice{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-2.5mu}{}\right|\mathchoice{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-2.5mu}{}\right|_{\infty}}:\mathcal{S}\subset\mathcal{X},\,0<\left|\mathchoice{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-2.5mu}{}\left|\mathchoice{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-2.5mu}{}\left|\mathcal{S}\right|\mathchoice{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-2.5mu}{}\right|\mathchoice{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-2.5mu}{}\right|_{\infty}<\infty\right\} (27)

denote the Jung constant of 𝒳\mathcal{X} [52, 53], i.e., the tightest multiplicative factor between the Chebyshev radius and diameter of any bounded subset of 𝒳\mathcal{X}. In Euclidean space 𝒳=ℝd\mathcal{X}=\mathbb{R}^{d}, we have γ≤d/(d+1)\gamma\leq d/(d+1) for a general norm ∥⋅∥\lVert{\mkern 2.0mu\cdot\mkern 2.0mu}\rVert [54, Theorem 6], and γ=1/2\gamma=1/2 for the ℓ∞\ell^{\infty}-norm [46, Section 5.3].

First, we present upper and lower bounds on the average extremal power-constrained Doeblin curve of KK (similar to [25]).55 5 The results in Section II-D supersede [1, Theorem 2 and Corollaries 1 and 2].

Theorem 2 (Bounds on Average Extremal Doeblin Curve).

The power-constrained Doeblin curve FK𝖠𝖤\mathrm{F}_{K}^{\mathsf{AE}} satisfies the upper and lower bounds t​θ​(𝟎,M−1​(p∕t))≤FK𝖠𝖤​(t,p)≤t​Θ𝑖𝑛𝑣𝑏𝑟𝑒𝑣𝑒​(2​γ​M−1​(p∕t))t\,\theta(\mathbf{0},M^{-1}(\ifrac{p}{t}))\leq\mathrm{F}_{K}^{\mathsf{AE}}(t;p)\leq t\,\invbreve{\Theta}(2\gamma\,M^{-1}(\ifrac{p}{t})) for all t∈(0,1]t\in(0,1], where θ\theta and Θ\Theta are defined in Equation 26, the Jung constant γ\gamma is defined in Equation 27, and MM is the power function.

The proof is provided in Section IV-C, utilizing the variational characterization of Doeblin coefficients from Theorem 1 and the maximal coupling characterization from Proposition 1.

If KK acts as a convolution operator on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} (e.g., additive noise), then θ⁡(a,s)\theta(a,s) is independent of aa, namely θ⁡(a,s)=Θ⁡(s)\theta(a,s)=\Theta(s) for all a∈𝒳a\in\mathcal{X}. This immediately leads to the following counterpart to [25, Corollary 5].

Corollary 1 (Average Extremal Doeblin Curves of Convolution Kernels).

For any kernel KK which acts as a convolution operator on 𝒳=𝒴=ℝd\mathcal{X}=\mathcal{Y}=\mathbb{R}^{d}, and for which Θ\Theta (defined in Equation 26) is concave, we have t​Θ​(M−1​(p∕t))≤FK𝖠𝖤​(t,p)≤t​Θ​((2​d/(d+1))​M−1​(p∕t))t\,\Theta(M^{-1}(\ifrac{p}{t}))\leq\mathrm{F}_{K}^{\mathsf{AE}}(t;p)\leq t\,\Theta(({2d}/{(d+1)})\,M^{-1}(\ifrac{p}{t})) for all t∈(0,1]t\in(0,1], where MM is the power function. Furthermore, if d=1d=1 or ∥⋅∥\lVert{\mkern 2.0mu\cdot\mkern 2.0mu}\rVert is the ℓ∞\ell^{\infty}-norm, then FK𝖠𝖤​(t,p)=t​Θ​(M−1​(p∕t))\mathrm{F}_{K}^{\mathsf{AE}}(t;p)=t\,\Theta(M^{-1}(\ifrac{p}{t})).

The equality in the d=1d=1 or ℓ∞\ell^{\infty}-norm case trivially follows, since the upper and lower bounds from Theorem 2 match. The next corollary provides three examples of closed-form Doeblin curves for convolution kernels on ℝ\mathbb{R}.

Corollary 2 (Examples of Average Extremal Doeblin Curves).

Consider the Gaussian, Laplace, and qq-Gaussian [55, Section 2.3] (q=2q=2) additive noise kernels on 𝒳=𝒴=ℝ\mathcal{X}=\mathcal{Y}=\mathbb{R}, given by

K1​(A|x;σ2)\displaystyle K_{1}(A\,|\,x\,;\>\sigma^{2}) =∫A1σ​2​π​exp⁡(−(y−x)22​σ2)​⁡𝑑y,\displaystyle=\int_{A}\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\left(-\frac{(y-x)^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}y, (28)
K2​(A|x;b)\displaystyle K_{2}(A\,|\,x\,;\>b) =∫A12​b​exp⁡(−|y−x|b)​⁡𝑑y,\displaystyle=\int_{A}\frac{1}{2b}\exp\left(-\frac{\left\lvert y-x\right\rvert}{b}\right)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}y, (29)

respectively. Then, under the norm ∥⋅∥=|⋅|\lVert{\mkern 2.0mu\cdot\mkern 2.0mu}\rVert=|{\mkern 2.0mu\cdot\mkern 2.0mu}| and power function M⁡(z)=z2M(z)=z^{2}, the average extremal power-constrained Doeblin curves for these kernels are

FK1𝖠𝖤​(t,p,σ2)\displaystyle\mathrm{F}_{K_{1}}^{\mathsf{AE}}(t;p,\sigma^{2}) =t⁡(1−2​Φ​(−1σ​pt)),\displaystyle=t\left(1-2\Phi\left(-\frac{1}{\sigma}\sqrt{\frac{p}{t}}\right)\right), (31)
FK2𝖠𝖤​(t,p,b)\displaystyle\mathrm{F}_{K_{2}}^{\mathsf{AE}}(t;p,b) =t⁡(1−exp⁡(−1b​pt)),\displaystyle=t\left(1-\exp\left(-\frac{1}{b}\sqrt{\frac{p}{t}}\right)\right), (32)

where Φ:ℝ→(0,1)\Phi\colon\mathbb{R}\rightarrow(0,1) denotes the standard Gaussian CDF Φ⁡(y)=∫−∞y(1∕2​π)​exp⁡(−t∕2∕2)​⁡𝑑t\Phi(y)=\int_{-\infty}^{y}(\ifrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}})\exp(-\ifrac{t^{2}}{2})\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t. Furthermore, the joint ranges 𝔉⁡(K1,𝒢p)\mathfrak{F}(K_{1};\mathcal{G}_{p}), 𝔉⁡(K2,𝒢p)\mathfrak{F}(K_{2};\mathcal{G}_{p}), and 𝔉⁡(K3,𝒢p)\mathfrak{F}(K_{3};\mathcal{G}_{p}) comprise the entire areas under the corresponding Doeblin curves, where 𝒢p\mathcal{G}_{p} is the set of all Markov kernels WW that satisfy |||W|||𝖠𝖤≤p|\mathchoice{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-2.5mu}{}\mathinner{|\mathchoice{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-2.5mu}{}\mathinner{|W|}\mathchoice{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-2.5mu}{}|}\mathchoice{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-2.5mu}{}|_{\mathsf{AE}}\leq p.

Corollary 2 is proved in Section IV-C. Note that [25] presents a similar result on the power-constrained Dobrushin curves of Gaussian additive noise kernels. By following the steps in this proof up to Equation 296, we obtain that Θ\Theta is concave for any convolution kernel on ℝ\mathbb{R} whose density function g⁡(z)=g⁡(x−y)=d​Kd​y​(y∣x)g(z)=g(x-y)=\frac{\mathrm{d}K}{\mathrm{d}y}(y\mid x) is symmetric about z=0z=0 and non-increasing on z∈[0,∞)z\in[0,\infty). For such convolution kernels, the Doeblin curve FK𝖠𝖤\mathrm{F}_{K}^{\mathsf{AE}} is concave in tt, since Corollary 1 establishes that FK𝖠𝖤\mathrm{F}_{K}^{\mathsf{AE}} is the perspective of the composition of a concave function Θ\Theta and a concave non-decreasing function M−1M^{-1} (cf. [25, Remark 4]).

Figure 2 presents Doeblin curves for the convolution kernels in Corollary 2 with σ2=1\sigma^{2}=1, b=1b=1, and β=1\beta=1. The trivial upper bound Equation 22 due to submultiplicativity of ρ\rho is depicted by all three curves remaining below the gray dotted line y=ty=t. Since the derivatives of all three curves approach 11 as t→0t\rightarrow 0, the complementary Doeblin coefficients for all three kernels are ρ⁡(K1)=ρ⁡(K2)=ρ⁡(K3)=1\rho(K_{1})=\rho(K_{2})=\rho(K_{3})=1. Hence, the contraction behavior of these kernels is only captured by their Doeblin curves through the analysis in Theorem 2 and the ensuing corollaries.

Lastly, we present bounds on the uniform average power-constrained Doeblin curve of a general kernel KK. To do so, we impose additional regularity structure by requiring all input kernels WW to have a fixed source space 𝒰\mathcal{U} with finiteness or boundedness assumptions. We also impose sub-Gaussianity assumptions on WW as required.

Proposition 7 (Upper Bound on Uniform Average Doeblin Curve).

Let 𝒰\mathcal{U} be a finite set. Let 𝒢\mathcal{G} be the set of all Markov kernels W:𝒰×ℱ𝒳→[0,1]W\colon\mathcal{U}\times\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{X}}\rightarrow[0,1] satisfying the following assumptions:

  1. 1.

    (Uniform average power constraint) |||W|||𝖴𝖠≤p|\mathchoice{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-2.5mu}{}\mathinner{|\mathchoice{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-2.5mu}{}\mathinner{|W|}\mathchoice{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-2.5mu}{}|}\mathchoice{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-2.5mu}{}|_{\mathsf{UA}}\leq p.

  2. 2.

    (Sub-Gaussianity) Consider the set of random variables {Zu}u∈𝒰\{Z_{u}\}_{u\in\mathcal{U}} given by Zu=M⁡(∥Xu∥)Z_{u}=M(\lVert X_{u}\rVert), Xu∼W(⋅∣u)X_{u}\sim W({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid u) for each u∈𝒰u\in\mathcal{U}. Then, there exists σ>0\sigma>0 such that for any u∈𝒰u\in\mathcal{U}, 𝔼⁡[exp⁡(λ⁡(Zu−𝔼⁡[Zu]))]≤exp⁡(σ∕2∕λ∕2∕2)\mathbb{E}\bigl[\exp(\lambda\left(Z_{u}-\mathbb{E}\left[Z_{u}\right]\right))\bigr]\leq\exp(\ifrac{\sigma^{2}\lambda^{2}}{2}) for all λ∈ℝ\lambda\in\mathbb{R}.

Then, the constrained Doeblin curve FK​(t,𝒢)\mathrm{F}_{K}(t;\mathcal{G}) satisfies the upper bound FK​(t,𝒢)≤t​Θ𝑖𝑛𝑣𝑏𝑟𝑒𝑣𝑒​(2​γ​M−1​((p+σ​2​loge​|𝒰|)/t))\mathrm{F}_{K}(t;\mathcal{G})\leq t\,\invbreve{\Theta}(2\gamma\,M^{-1}({(p+\sigma\sqrt{2\log_{e}\left\lvert\mathcal{U}\right\rvert})}/{t})) for all t∈(0,1]t\in(0,1] where Θ\Theta is defined in Equation 26, the Jung constant γ\gamma is defined in Equation 27, and MM is the power function.

Proposition 8 (Upper Bound on Uniform Average Doeblin Curve).

Let (𝒰,d𝒰)(\mathcal{U},d_{\mathcal{U}}) be a Polish space endowed with a metric d𝒰:𝒰×𝒰→ℝ+d_{\mathcal{U}}\colon\mathcal{U}\times\mathcal{U}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{+} such that (𝒰,d𝒰)(\mathcal{U},d_{\mathcal{U}}) is totally bounded, i.e., the ϵ\epsilon-covering number N(ϵ,𝒰,d𝒰)≜min{n∈ℕ:∃{u1∗,...,un∗}⊆𝒰,∀u∈𝒰,∃i∈[n],d𝒰(u,ui∗)≤ϵ}N(\epsilon,\mathcal{U},d_{\mathcal{U}})\triangleq\min\{n\in\mathbb{N}:\exists\{u^{*}_{1},\mathinner{\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp},u^{*}_{n}\}\subseteq\mathcal{U},\forall u\in\mathcal{U},\,\exists i\in[n],\,d_{\mathcal{U}}(u,u^{*}_{i})\leq\epsilon\} is finite for all ϵ>0\epsilon>0. We provide examples of non-trivial kernels satisfying the preconditions of Propositions 7 and 8 in Appendix C.

III Main Results on Applications

In this section, we present three illustrative applications of Doeblin curves to other areas of information theory and learning theory. Firstly, we derive generalization error bounds for iterative optimization algorithms operating over unbounded feasible sets. Secondly, we establish lower bounds for reliable computation using circuits of noisy qq-ary gates. Lastly, we introduce a new definition of (ϵ,δ)(\epsilon,\delta)-differential privacy based on our variational characterization of Doeblin coefficients, and provide improved privacy bounds for online iterative optimization. The applications showcase how Doeblin curves can provide nontrivial guarantees even when strong data processing constants such as the Dobrushin coefficient or the mutual information contraction coefficient degenerate to 11 and do not provide any useful information. While our results on generalization error can be specialized to use Dobrushin curves (see footnote 6 below), the latter two applications rely on Doeblin curves to trace the contraction between a collection of probability distributions, which cannot be done with Dobrushin curves (which can only analyze the contraction between two distributions).

III-A Bounds on Generalization Error

In this subsection, we use Doeblin curves to extend existing information-theoretic generalization error bounds for noisy iterative optimization algorithms in [41] to settings where the feasible set has infinite diameter or the optimization problem is unconstrained altogether (also see [56]). We utilize the information-theoretic framework introduced in [41], which provides generalization error bounds for compact feasible sets by leveraging the Dobrushin contraction coefficient of additive noise channels. Their results indicate that data points used in earlier iterations have a decaying contribution to the generalization error due to the cumulative effect of noise injection, with the rate of decay governed by the Dobrushin coefficient of the underlying noise channel. This analysis yields a non-trivial bound only when the feasible set has finite diameter, since the Dobrushin coefficient trivially equals 11 otherwise. To address feasible sets with infinite diameter, we utilize Doeblin curves as a finer-grained tool to capture information decay for data points used in earlier iterations even when Dobrushin coefficients fail to do so, thereby yielding non-trivial generalization error bounds despite the absence of coarser coefficient-based contraction.66 6 In all applications of Doeblin curves, suitable constraints may be placed on the Doeblin curve to obtain tighter bounds by incorporating prior knowledge about the input distributions. For example, when deriving our results on generalization error, we only utilize the Doeblin curve FΦ𝖴𝖠\mathrm{F}_{\Phi}^{\mathsf{UA}} of the additive noise mechanism to quantify the contraction between two distributions pushed through the mechanism. Hence, we may instead consider the constrained curve which only includes input kernels with |𝒰|=2|\mathcal{U}|=2, which reduces to the Dobrushin curve of the noise mechanism. Nonetheless, we present all results in this paper in terms of the more general Doeblin curve FΦ𝖴𝖠\mathrm{F}_{\Phi}^{\mathsf{UA}} for conceptual simplicity.

Formally, following [41], we begin by considering a general (possibly non-convex) stochastic optimization problem,

minw∈𝒲⁡Gμ​(w),\displaystyle\min_{w\in\mathcal{W}}G_{\mu}(w),
whereGμ​(w)≜𝔼Z∼μ[g⁡(w,Z)]=∫𝒵g⁡(w,⋅)​⁡𝑑μ,\displaystyle\text{where}\quad G_{\mu}(w)\triangleq\mathop{\mathbb{E}}_{Z\sim\mu}\left[g(w,Z)\right]=\int_{\mathcal{Z}}g(w,{\mkern 2.0mu\cdot\mkern 2.0mu})\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu,

where w∈𝒲⊆ℝdw\in\mathcal{W}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} are the model parameters constrained to the (potentially unbounded) feasible set 𝒲\mathcal{W}, μ\mu is the underlying data distribution over the samples ZZ belonging to the sample space 𝒵\mathcal{Z}, and g:𝒲×𝒵→ℝ+g\colon\mathcal{W}\times\mathcal{Z}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{+} is the loss function. In practice, the true data distribution μ\mu is usually unknown, and only a dataset 𝒮≜(Z1,...,Zn)\mathcal{S}\triangleq({Z}_{1},\mathinner{\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp},{Z}_{n}) consisting of nn independent and identically distributed samples Zi∼μ{Z}_{i}\sim\mu is available. Thus, we instead consider the empirical risk minimization (ERM) problem

with the aim of finding a solution which generalizes well to the original problem of minimizing GμG_{\mu}. To this end, we consider the following noisy iterative algorithm. The algorithm is initialized with an arbitrary parameter W0∈𝒲W_{0}\in\mathcal{W}. Next, the algorithm performs TT iterations by updating the parameters WtW_{t} according to the rule

However, since w∗w^{*} is unknown in practice, we use the worst-case bounds on the second moment of the iterates instead.

III-B Reliable Computation Using Noisy qq-ary Gates

In this subsection, we use Doeblin curves to establish information-theoretic bounds on the expressive power of circuits of noisy gates for the computation of qq-ary functions. This builds on results for Boolean functions in [25]. We consider nn-input circuits which compute a single output value using bb-input gates, where the result of each gate is perturbed by independent noise. Historically, the study of such architectures began with von Neumann’s pioneering work on fault-tolerant Boolean circuits [57, 58, 59], and has been largely limited to binary operations. We expand this line of study to multivalued logic systems, as motivated by recent advancements in classical and quantum information processing [60].

Formally, we model a noisy circuit over a qq-ary alphabet 𝒬={ξ1,...,ξq}⊂ℝd\mathcal{Q}=\{\xi_{1},\mathinner{\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp},\xi_{q}\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} as a directed acyclic graph with nn input vertices X1,...,Xn∈𝒬X_{1},\mathinner{\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp},X_{n}\in\mathcal{Q} indexed by i∈[n]i\in[n]. The inputs are processed by a collection of mm gate vertices indexed by j∈[m]j\in[m], each of which takes bj≤bb_{j}\leq b ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}-valued arguments and computes a 𝒬\mathcal{Q}-valued result Zj∈𝒬Z_{j}\in\mathcal{Q}, which is then corrupted by independent noise from some arbitrary fixed kernel Φ\Phi to produce Yj∈ℝdY_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. Formally, letting 𝒩j\mathcal{N}_{j} and ℳj\mathcal{M}_{j} denote the incoming edge sets of input vertices and gate vertices feeding into gate jj, respectively, we have

Zj≜Γj({Xi}i∈𝒩j,{Yj′}j′∈ℳj),Yj∼Φ(⋅∣Zj)Z_{j}\triangleq\Gamma_{j}\left(\left\{X_{i}\right\}_{i\in\mathcal{N}_{j}},\left\{Y_{j^{\prime}}\right\}_{j^{\prime}\in\mathcal{M}_{j}}\right),\quad Y_{j}\sim\Phi({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid Z_{j}) (46)

for some deterministic gate function Γj:(ℝd)bj→𝒬\Gamma_{j}\colon(\mathbb{R}^{d})^{b_{j}}\rightarrow\mathcal{Q}, where bj=|𝒩j|+|ℳj|≤bb_{j}=|\mathcal{N}_{j}|+|\mathcal{M}_{j}|\leq b. Without loss of generality, we assume the gates are indexed in topological order, i.e., ℳj⊆[j−1]\mathcal{M}_{j}\subseteq[j-1] for each j∈[m]j\in[m]. At the end, the circuit produces a single output vertex YmY_{m} with no outgoing edges. We assume there exists a directed path from each XiX_{i} to YmY_{m}, so none of the circuit inputs are discarded. We note that this model can be seen as a qq-ary generalization of the setup considered in [25, Section 5.3].

One goal of such a circuit is to compute a function G:𝒬n→𝒬G\colon\mathcal{Q}^{n}\rightarrow\mathcal{Q} with error probability at most P𝖾𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋>0\mathrm{P}_{\mathsf{error}}>0. Namely, there must exist some fixed decoding function G^:ℝd→𝒬\hat{G}\colon\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathcal{Q} such that for any input vector (x1,...,xn)∈𝒬n(x_{1},\mathinner{\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp},x_{n})\in\mathcal{Q}^{n}, ℙ⁡(G^​(Ym)=G⁡(x1,...,xn))≥1−P𝖾𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋\mathbb{P}(\hat{G}(Y_{m})=G(x_{1},\mathinner{\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp},x_{n}))\geq 1-\mathrm{P}_{\mathsf{error}}, where the probability is taken with respect to all the noise in the circuit. In the binary case (q=|𝒬|=2q=|\mathcal{Q}|=2), by Le Cam’s relation, the error probability of the optimal decoder can be controlled by the TV distance between the marginal distributions of YmY_{m} induced by setting some “initial” input vertex to 00 or 11, respectively, while fixing all other input values [25, Eq. 146]. So, several works study the question of how information measures contract over fault-tolerant circuits, e.g., [25] recursively upper-bounds TV distance while [9] bounds mutual information. Propelled by such analyses, and in light of the interpretation of complementary Doeblin coefficients as a multi-way generalization of TV distance [19, Theorem 2], we analyze the complementary Doeblin coefficient of the qq induced marginal distributions of YmY_{m} as a first step towards understanding information propagation in noisy qq-ary circuits. (Intuitively, perceiving a circuit as a Markov chain, the analysis of TV distance in [25] is related to the coupling time of two copies of the chain with two different values at the “initial” vertex [61]. On the other hand, our analysis of Doeblin coefficients is related to the coupling time of qq copies of the chain initiated at all qq possible values.) Our main contribution is the following theorem, which relates the Doeblin coefficient to the noise mechanism’s Doeblin curve.

Theorem 4 (Upper Bound on Circuit Output Divergence).

Fix ϵ>0\epsilon>0. For all nn-input circuits of noisy bb-input gates with sufficiently large nn, there exists some input vertex, which we take to be X1X_{1} without loss of generality, such that for any fixed values x2,...,xn∈𝒬x_{2},\mathinner{\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp},x_{n}\in\mathcal{Q} of the remaining inputs,

ρ⁡([PYm(1),...,PYm(q)])≤max⁡{t∈[0,1]:FinvbreveΦ𝖴𝖠​(min⁡{1,b​t},p)=t}+ϵ,\rho\Bigl(\bigl[P_{Y_{m}}^{(1)},\mathinner{\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp},P_{Y_{m}}^{(q)}\bigr]\Bigr)\\ \leq\max\left\{t\in[0,1]:\invbreve{\mathrm{F}}_{\Phi}^{\mathsf{UA}}\left(\min\left\{1,bt\right\};p\right)=t\right\}+\epsilon, (47)

where PYm(ℓ)P_{Y_{m}}^{(\ell)} is the marginal distribution of YmY_{m} induced by the circuit when setting X1=ℓX_{1}=\ell and Xi=xiX_{i}=x_{i} for all i>1i>1, FΦ𝖴𝖠\mathrm{F}_{\Phi}^{\mathsf{UA}} is the uniform average power-constrained Doeblin curve of the noise kernel Φ\Phi for some norm ∥⋅∥\lVert{\mkern 2.0mu\cdot\mkern 2.0mu}\rVert on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} and power function M:ℝ+→ℝ+M\colon\mathbb{R}_{+}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{+}, and p≜maxξ∈𝒬⁡M⁡(‖ξ‖)p\triangleq\max_{\xi\in\mathcal{Q}}M\left(\left\lVert\xi\right\rVert\right).

Theorem 4 represents an information-theoretic limit on the quality of any output decoder, since decoding performance improves as output divergence increases. We defer the proof to Section V-B. The proof constructs a coupling of the induced marginal distributions at each gate output YjY_{j}, using the maximal coupling characterization of Doeblin coefficients Equation 68 to refine the couplings from earlier gates. This is formalized in the following lemma. For notational convenience, we denote collections of superscripted variables as w(1:q)=(w(1),...,w(q))w^{(1:q)}=(w^{(1)},\mathinner{\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp},w^{(q)}).

Lemma 3 (Stepwise Coupling Construction).

Let 𝒰\mathcal{U} be a finite subset of a separable Banach space. Let (𝒱,ℱ𝒱)(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{V}}) be a Polish space and let Φ:𝒰×ℱ𝒱→[0,1]\Phi\colon\mathcal{U}\times\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{V}}\rightarrow[0,1] be a Markov kernel from 𝒰\mathcal{U} to 𝒱\mathcal{V}. Let PU(1),...,PU(q)P_{U}^{(1)},\mathinner{\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp},P_{U}^{(q)} be a collection of probability measures on 𝒰\mathcal{U}, and let PV(1),...,PV(q)P_{V}^{(1)},\mathinner{\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp},P_{V}^{(q)} be the respective probability measures on 𝒱\mathcal{V} induced by pushing PU(ℓ)P_{U}^{(\ell)} through Φ\Phi for each ℓ∈[q]\ell\in[q], i.e.,

∀A∈ℱ𝒱,PV(ℓ)​(A)≜∫𝒰Φ⁡(A∣u)​⁡d​PU(ℓ)​(u).\forall A\in\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{V}},\quad P_{V}^{(\ell)}(A)\triangleq\int_{\mathcal{U}}\Phi(A\mid u)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}P_{U}^{(\ell)}(u). (48)

Then, given any coupling πU\pi_{U} of PU(1),...,PU(q)P_{U}^{(1)},\mathinner{\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp},P_{U}^{(q)}, there exists a coupling πV\pi_{V} of PV(1),...,PV(q)P_{V}^{(1)},\mathinner{\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp},P_{V}^{(q)} satisfying

ℙV(1:q)∼πV(¬(V(1)=⋅⋅⋅=V(q)))≤FinvbreveΦ𝖴𝖠(ℙU(1:q)∼πU(¬(U(1)=⋅⋅⋅=U(q)));p),\mathop{\mathbb{P}}_{V^{(1:q)}\sim\pi_{V}}\left(\lnot\left(V^{(1)}=\mathinner{\cdotp\mkern-2.0mu\cdotp\mkern-2.0mu\cdotp}=V^{(q)}\right)\right)\\ \leq\invbreve{\mathrm{F}}_{\Phi}^{\mathsf{UA}}\left(\mathop{\mathbb{P}}_{U^{(1:q)}\sim\pi_{U}}\left(\lnot\left(U^{(1)}=\mathinner{\cdotp\mkern-2.0mu\cdotp\mkern-2.0mu\cdotp}=U^{(q)}\right)\right);p\right),\ignorespaces\ignorespaces (49)

where we define p≜maxu∈𝒰⁡M⁡(‖u‖)p\triangleq\max_{u\in\mathcal{U}}M(\left\lVert u\right\rVert).

Lemma 3 is proved in Section V-B by constructing πV\pi_{V} as the weighted average (with respect to U(1:q)∼πUU^{(1:q)}\sim\pi_{U}) of the maximal coupling Equation 68 of Φ(⋅∣U(1)),...,Φ(⋅∣U(q))\Phi({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid U^{(1)}),\mathinner{\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp},\Phi({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid U^{(q)}). Iterating this construction for each gate leads to repeated application of the Doeblin curve FΦ𝖴𝖠\mathrm{F}_{\Phi}^{\mathsf{UA}}, which converges to the greatest fixed point of a transformed version of FΦ𝖴𝖠\mathrm{F}_{\Phi}^{\mathsf{UA}}.

III-C Relation to Differential Privacy and Online Algorithms

In this subsection, we utilize our variational characterization of Doeblin coefficients to motivate a new definition of group local differential privacy (LDP). Recall that a mechanism K:𝒳×ℱ𝒴→[0,1]K\colon\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}}\rightarrow[0,1], which is nothing but a Markov kernel, is (ϵ,δ)(\epsilon,\delta)-LDP if for any inputs x,x′∈𝒳x,x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X} both K(⋅∣x)K({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid x) and K(⋅∣x′)K({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid x^{\prime}) exhibit similar distributions [62, 63, 42, 64, 65, 66],99 9 This differs slightly from the standard definition of (central) differential privacy (DP), which considers input datasets of multiple users differing by only one user [67, Definition 2.4]. i.e.,

∀x,x′∈𝒳;∀A∈ℱ𝒴,K⁡(A∣x)−eϵ​K​(A∣x′)≤δ.\forall x,x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X};\,\forall A\in\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}},\quad K(A\mid x)-e^{\epsilon}K(A\mid x^{\prime})\leq\delta. (50)

Subtracting both sides from 11, this is equivalent to

∀x,x′∈𝒳;∀A∈ℱ𝒴,K⁡(Ac∣x)+eϵ​K​(A∣x′)≥1−δ.\displaystyle\forall x,x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X};\,\forall A\in\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}},\quad K(A^{\mathrm{c}}\mid x)+e^{\epsilon}K(A\mid x^{\prime})\geq 1-\delta. (51)

This rearrangement has an interesting interpretation: Consider a binary hypothesis testing scenario that aims to distinguish whether the output YY of a mechanism is derived from the distribution K(⋅∣x)K({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid x) versus K(⋅∣x′)K({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid x^{\prime}) for any fixed xx and x′x^{\prime}. Let A⊆𝒴A\subseteq\mathcal{Y} be any possible choice of the rejection region for the hypothesis Y∼K(⋅∣x′)Y\sim K({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid x^{\prime}). The reformulated version in Equation 51 essentially highlights the impossibility of achieving a very low weighted sum of type-I and type-II errors from the data YY derived from a differentially private mechanism KK (see [68, Theorem 2.1] for more details).

In addition, observe that the left-hand side of Equation 50 is bounded by an ϵ\epsilon-weighted TV distance (called the 𝖤γ\mathsf{E}_{\gamma}-divergence) between K(⋅∣x)K({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid x) and K(⋅∣x′)K({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid x^{\prime}). Indeed, this connection has been noted by, e.g., [42, 69]. Considering that 𝖤γ\mathsf{E}_{\gamma}-divergence, a weighted variant of TV distance (or Dobrushin coefficient), exactly characterizes local differential privacy, it is natural to ask whether a similarly weighted variant of the Doeblin coefficient can admit an analogous interpretation.

Motivated by this observation and our variational characterization of Doeblin coefficients from Theorem 1, we extend the standard definition of LDP to a ‘‘group’’ setting.1010 10 Accordingly, this is different from the usual definition of group DP based on distance between the input datasets [67, Theorem 2.2]. Consider any group size n≥2n\geq 2 and any ϵ=(ϵ1,...,ϵn)∈ℝ+n\boldsymbol{\epsilon}=(\epsilon_{1},\mathinner{\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp},\epsilon_{n})\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{n} where we assume without loss of generality that ϵ1=0\epsilon_{1}=0 and ϵi≤ϵj\epsilon_{i}\leq\epsilon_{j} for all i<ji<j . A mechanism KK is said to be (ϵ,δ,n)(\boldsymbol{\epsilon},\delta,n)-LDP if for any x1,...,xn∈𝒳x_{1},\mathinner{\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp},x_{n}\in\mathcal{X} and any ℱ𝒴\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}}-measurable nn-partition A1,...,AnA_{1},\mathinner{\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp},A_{n} of 𝒴\mathcal{Y},

∑i=1neϵi​K​(Ai∣xi)≥1−δ.\sum_{i=1}^{n}e^{\epsilon_{i}}K(A_{i}\mid x_{i})\geq 1-\delta. (52)

This definition may be interpreted in the context of an nn-ary hypothesis testing problem. Given a set of nn hypotheses Hi:Y∼K(⋅∣xi)H_{i}\colon Y\sim K({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid x_{i}) indexed by i∈[n]i\in[n], where YY is the observed variable, the generalized definition in Equation 52 states that the problem of identifying a single false hypothesis has a large weighted sum error for any possible choices of rejection regions. Any reasonable test for this hypothesis testing problem would partition the space 𝒴\mathcal{Y} into nn rejection regions A1,...,AnA_{1},\mathinner{\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp},A_{n}, and the test rejects hypothesis HiH_{i} if YY takes on a value in AiA_{i}. Therefore, K⁡(Ai∣xi)K(A_{i}\mid x_{i}) represents the conditional probability of error given HiH_{i} in this scenario. For n=2n=2, the notion of (ϵ,δ,2)(\boldsymbol{\epsilon},\delta,2)-LDP reduces to the standard definition in Equation 50. Furthermore, KK being (ϵ,δ,n)(\boldsymbol{\epsilon},\delta,n)-LDP for n≥2n\geq 2 is a stronger condition, as it implies that KK is also ([ϵ1,...,ϵm],δ,m)([\epsilon_{1},\mathinner{\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp},\epsilon_{m}],\delta,m)-LDP for all 2≤m≤n2\leq m\leq n. Intuitively, while an (ϵ,δ)(\epsilon,\delta)-LDP algorithm makes it difficult for an attacker to distinguish between a pair of inputs, an (ϵ,δ,n)(\boldsymbol{\epsilon},\delta,n)-LDP algorithm protects against arbitrary nn-way comparisons between inputs, which is a stronger notion.

Motivated by this formulation, we define weighted analogues of the Doeblin and complementary Doeblin coefficients for a Markov kernel K:𝒳×ℱ𝒴→[0,1]K\colon\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}}\rightarrow[0,1]:

τϵ​(K,n)\displaystyle\tau_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}(K,n) ≜infx1,…,xn∈𝒳infn-partition of 𝒴A1,…,An∑i=1neϵi​K​(Ai∣xi),\displaystyle\triangleq\inf_{x_{1},\dots,x_{n}\in\mathcal{X}}\inf_{\begin{subarray}{c}\text{$n$-partition of $\mathcal{Y}$}\\ A_{1},\dots,A_{n}\end{subarray}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}e^{\epsilon_{i}}K(A_{i}\mid x_{i}),\, (53)
ρϵ​(K,n)\displaystyle\rho_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}(K,n) ≜1−τϵ​(K,n).\displaystyle\triangleq 1-\tau_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}(K,n). (54)

We remark that τϵ​(K,n)∈[0,1]\tau_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}(K,n)\in[0,1] (and so ρϵ​(K,n)∈[0,1]\rho_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}(K,n)\in[0,1]), because for any x1,...,xn∈𝒳x_{1},\mathinner{\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp},x_{n}\in\mathcal{X}, we have

τϵ​(K,n)\displaystyle\tau_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}(K,n) ≤(a)eϵ1​K​(𝒴∣x1)+∑i=2neϵi​K​(∅∣xi)\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(a)}}}{{\leq}}e^{\epsilon_{1}}K(\mathcal{Y}\mid x_{1})+\sum_{i=2}^{n}e^{\epsilon_{i}}K(\emptyset\mid x_{i}) (55)
=(b)K⁡(𝒴∣x1)=(c)1,\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(b)}}}{{=}}K(\mathcal{Y}\mid x_{1})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(c)}}}{{=}}1, (56)

where (a) holds by upper-bounding the infima in Equation 53 with a specific instance, (b) holds because ϵ1=0\epsilon_{1}=0, and (c) holds because KK is a Markov kernel. Moreover, akin to how [69, 42] reformulated local differential privacy in terms of the 𝖤γ\mathsf{E}_{\gamma} contraction coefficient,1111 11 We note that the 𝖤γ\mathsf{E}_{\gamma}-divergence is a weighted version of TV distance, which is equivalent (when appropriately scaled) to Bayes statistical information or DeGroot distance [70]. ρϵ​(K,n)\rho_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}(K,n) captures (ϵ,δ,n)(\boldsymbol{\epsilon},\delta,n)-LDP exactly: ρϵ​(K,n)≤δ\rho_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}(K,n)\leq\delta if and only if KK is (ϵ,δ,n)(\boldsymbol{\epsilon},\delta,n)-LDP (see proof of Theorem 5 in Section V-C).

In addition, we note a connection between ρϵ\rho_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}} and the concept of min-DeGroot distance from [19], which is construed as a generalization of Bayes statistical information. In this context, a hidden random variable X∈𝒳X\in\mathcal{X} (where 𝒳={x1,...,xn}\mathcal{X}=\{x_{1},\mathinner{\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp},x_{n}\} has cardinality |𝒳|=n|\mathcal{X}|=n) follows a prior distribution 𝝀∈ℝn\boldsymbol{\lambda}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, and a random variable Y∈𝒴Y\in\mathcal{Y} is observed according to an observation model denoted by KK. Let X^∈𝒳\hat{X}\in\mathcal{X} be any (possibly randomized) estimator of XX based on YY, such that X→Y→X^X\rightarrow Y\rightarrow\hat{X} forms a Markov chain. [19] defines the min-DeGroot distance τmin​(𝝀,K)\tau_{\min}(\boldsymbol{\lambda},K) as the reduction in Bayes risk when observing the data YY compared to not observing YY. Specifically,

τmin(𝝀,K)≜mini∈[n]λi−∫𝒴(mini∈[n]λi⁡d​K⁡d​μ(⋅∣xi))dμ,\displaystyle\tau_{\min}(\boldsymbol{\lambda},K)\triangleq\min_{i\in[n]}\lambda_{i}-\int_{\mathcal{Y}}\left(\min_{i\in[n]}\lambda_{i}\frac{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}K}{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu}({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid x_{i})\right)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu, (57)

where μ\mu is the common dominating measure for K(⋅∣x1),...,K(⋅∣xn)K({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid x_{1}),\allowbreak\mathinner{\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp},K({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid x_{n}) from Equation 6. By setting λi=eϵi/∑i=1neϵi\lambda_{i}=e^{\epsilon_{i}}/\sum_{i=1}^{n}e^{\epsilon_{i}} and applying Proposition 2, the min-DeGroot distance can be interpreted as a rescaled version of ρϵ​(K,n)\rho_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}(K,n), namely,

ρϵ​(K,n)=(∑i=1neϵi)​τmin​(𝝀,K).\displaystyle\rho_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}(K,n)=\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}e^{\epsilon_{i}}\right)\tau_{\min}(\boldsymbol{\lambda},K). (58)

Therefore, the definition of (ϵ,δ,n)(\boldsymbol{\epsilon},\delta,n)-LDP is essentially a rescaled version of the generalized notion of Bayes statistical information obtained from the set {x1,...,xn}\{x_{1},\mathinner{\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp},x_{n}\}. Our proposed definition of an (ϵ,δ,n)(\boldsymbol{\epsilon},\delta,n)-LDP mechanism underscores that, given the processed data of the entire group, obtaining any substantial “information” (quantified in the Bayes statistical information sense) about any individual member is “hard.”

In the following theorem, we prove contraction properties of ρϵ​(K,n)\rho_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}(K,n). By Equation 58, these results translate to contraction properties of τmin​(𝝀,K)\tau_{\min}(\boldsymbol{\lambda},K).

Theorem 5 (Contraction of ρϵ​(K,n)\rho_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}(K,n)).

Let K:𝒳×ℱ𝒴→[0,1]K\colon\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}}\rightarrow[0,1] be an absolutely continuous Markov kernel. For any group size n≥2n\geq 2 and any ϵ=(ϵ1,...,ϵn)∈ℝ+n\boldsymbol{\epsilon}=(\epsilon_{1},\mathinner{\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp},\epsilon_{n})\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{n} such that ϵ1=0\epsilon_{1}=0 and ϵi≤ϵj\epsilon_{i}\leq\epsilon_{j} for all i<ji<j, we have the following properties:

  1. 1.

    (Submultiplicativity) For any Markov kernel W:𝒰×ℱ𝒳→[0,1]W\colon\mathcal{U}\times\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{X}}\rightarrow[0,1],

    ρϵ​(W​K,n)≤ρϵ​(W,n)​ρϵ​(K,n).\displaystyle\rho_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}(WK,n)\leq\rho_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}(W,n)\,\rho_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}(K,n). (59)
  2. 2.

    (Contraction behavior) KK is (ϵ,δ,n)(\boldsymbol{\epsilon},\delta,n)-LDP iff for any Markov kernel W:𝒰×ℱ𝒳→[0,1]W\colon\mathcal{U}\times\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{X}}\rightarrow[0,1],

    ρϵ​(W​K,n)≤δ​ρϵ​(W,n).\displaystyle\rho_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}(WK,n)\leq\delta\rho_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}(W,n). (60)
  3. 3.

    (Doeblin curves) For any Markov kernel W:𝒰×ℱ𝒳→[0,1]W\colon\mathcal{U}\times\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{X}}\rightarrow[0,1] satisfying |||W|||𝖴𝖠≤p|\mathchoice{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-2.5mu}{}\mathinner{|\mathchoice{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-2.5mu}{}\mathinner{|W|}\mathchoice{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-2.5mu}{}|}\mathchoice{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-2.5mu}{}|_{\mathsf{UA}}\leq p,

    ρϵ​(W​K,n)≤FK𝖴𝖠​(ρϵ​(W,n),p).\displaystyle\rho_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}(WK,n)\leq\mathrm{F}_{K}^{\mathsf{UA}}(\rho_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}(W,n);p). (61)

Theorem 5 is proved in Section V-C. Parts 1 and 2 imply that ρϵ\rho_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}} exhibits contraction-coefficient-like properties akin to ρ\rho, with Part 1 acting as a meta-SDPI for ρϵ\rho_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}} (cf. [16, Proposition 3]) and Part 2 characterizing δ\delta as the contraction coefficient of this meta-SDPI. In particular, the data processing inequality for ρϵ\rho_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}, i.e.,

ρϵ​(W​K,n)≤ρϵ​(W,n),\rho_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}(WK,n)\leq\rho_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}(W,n), (62)

is an immediate consequence due to ρϵ​(K,n)∈[0,1]\rho_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}(K,n)\in[0,1]. In addition, considering the connection between ρϵ\rho_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}} and the min-DeGroot distance highlighted above, Part 1 can be restated as an SDPI for min-DeGroot distances, i.e., for any Markov kernel W:𝒰×ℱ𝒳→[0,1]W\colon\mathcal{U}\times\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{X}}\rightarrow[0,1] with finite 𝒰\mathcal{U}, τmin​(𝝀,W​K)≤ρϵ​(K,|𝒰|)​τmin​(𝝀,W)\tau_{\min}(\boldsymbol{\lambda},WK)\leq\rho_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}(K,\left\lvert\mathcal{U}\right\rvert)\,\tau_{\min}(\boldsymbol{\lambda},W).

Equation Equation 61 and the techniques developed above provide tools for tighter privacy guarantees for various mechanisms. Using these results, we now derive differential privacy guarantees for online iterative algorithms using Doeblin curves. While prior works such as [69] rely on compactness assumptions, our focus is on extending such analyses to potentially unbounded spaces where it can be difficult to capture privacy using classical contraction-coefficient-based techniques. To this end, we consider and build on the online learning framework presented in [69, Section IV-B], where the learner sequentially minimizes a sequence of convex objectives {gt}t=1n\{g_{t}\}_{t=1}^{n} over a parameter space 𝒲⊆ℝd\mathcal{W}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}. The protocol proceeds as follows. The learner initializes with a random parameter W0∈𝒲W_{0}\in\mathcal{W}, and at each iteration t∈[T]t\in[T], the cost function gtg_{t} is revealed. The learner then performs the update

Wt≜proj𝒲(Wt−1−ηt∇gt(Wt−1)+mtNt),W_{t}\triangleq\proj_{\mathcal{W}}\left(W_{t-1}-\eta_{t}\nabla g_{t}(W_{t-1})+m_{t}N_{t}\right), (63)

where the projection operator proj𝒲\proj_{\mathcal{W}} ensures that the parameters remain within the feasible set 𝒲\mathcal{W},1212 12 As before, our results hold with proj𝒲\proj_{\mathcal{W}} being any function whose range is 𝒲\mathcal{W}. ηt>0\eta_{t}>0 is the learning rate, and mtm_{t} scales the standard Gaussian noise Nt∼𝖭𝗈𝗋𝗆𝖺𝗅⁡(0,I)N_{t}\sim\mathsf{Normal}(0,I) (where II is the identity matrix of appropriate dimension). By taking gt​(w)≜ℓ⁡(w,Zt)g_{t}(w)\triangleq\ell(w,Z_{t}) where ℓ:𝒲×𝒵→ℝ+\ell\colon\mathcal{W}\times\mathcal{Z}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{+} is a loss function, this framework subsumes one-pass ERM, where the learner approximates the solution of minw∈𝒲⁡1T​∑t=1Tℓ⁡(w,Zt)\min_{w\in\mathcal{W}}\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\ell(w,Z_{t}) with data points Z1,...,ZT∈𝒵Z_{1},\mathinner{\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp},Z_{T}\in\mathcal{Z} revealed sequentially. The goal is to ensure that the final iterate WTW_{T} satisfies a privacy guarantee. We assume the gradient of each objective gtg_{t} is uniformly bounded, i.e.,

∀t∈[T],∀w∈𝒲,‖∇gt​(w)‖2≤L.\forall t\in[T],\,\forall w\in\mathcal{W},\quad\left\lVert\nabla g_{t}(w)\right\rVert_{2}\leq L. (64)

Existing LDP guarantees for online algorithms [69] rely on the contraction coefficient of 𝖤γ\mathsf{E}_{\gamma}-divergence, which quantifies the decay of information due to additive noise. However, for 𝒲\mathcal{W} with infinite diameter, the contraction coefficient for 𝖤γ\mathsf{E}_{\gamma}-divergence degenerates to 11. Below, we utilize the contraction bound on ρϵ\rho_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}} in terms of Doeblin curves FΦ𝖴𝖠\mathrm{F}_{\Phi}^{\mathsf{UA}} from Theorem 5 to quantify the contraction induced by the noise NtN_{t}.

Theorem 6 (Differential Privacy for Unconstrained Online Learning).

Let W0(i)∼PW0(i)W_{0}^{(i)}\sim P_{W_{0}}^{(i)} for i∈[n]i\in[n] denote nn different initializations of the online learning process. Let WT(i)∼PWT(i)W_{T}^{(i)}\sim P_{W_{T}}^{(i)} be the respective output parameters after TT iterations of the update rule Equation 63. Let FΦ𝖴𝖠\mathrm{F}_{\Phi}^{\mathsf{UA}} be the uniform average power-constrained Doeblin curve (with power function M⁡(z)=z2M(z)=z^{2}) of the 𝖭𝗈𝗋𝗆𝖺𝗅⁡(0,I)\mathsf{Normal}(0,I) additive noise channel. Then,

ρϵ​([PWT(1),...,PWT(n)],n)≤FΦ𝖴𝖠​(⋅⋅⋅​FΦ𝖴𝖠​(ρϵ​([PW0(1),...,PW0(n)],n),p1)​⋅⋅⋅,pT),\rho_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\left(\left[P_{W_{T}}^{(1)},\mathinner{\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp},P_{W_{T}}^{(n)}\right],n\right)\\ \leq\mathrm{F}_{\Phi}^{\mathsf{UA}}\biggl(\mathinner{\cdotp\mkern-2.0mu\cdotp\mkern-2.0mu\cdotp}\mathrm{F}_{\Phi}^{\mathsf{UA}}\biggl(\rho_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\left(\left[P_{W_{0}}^{(1)},\mathinner{\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp},P_{W_{0}}^{(n)}\right],n\right);p_{1}\biggr)\mathinner{\cdotp\mkern-2.0mu\cdotp\mkern-2.0mu\cdotp};p_{T}\biggr),\ignorespaces\ignorespaces (65)

where for each t∈[T]t\in[T] we define

pt≜1mt2​(2​maxi∈[n]⁡𝔼⁡[‖Wt−1(i)‖22]+2​ηt2​L2).p_{t}\triangleq\frac{1}{m_{t}^{2}}\left(2\max_{i\in[n]}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\lVert W_{t-1}^{(i)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right]+2\eta_{t}^{2}L^{2}\right). (66)

Theorem 6 is proved in Section V-C using Theorem 5, Part 3. We note that the above result can also be used to derive privacy amplification bounds for online learning algorithms as in [69] for more general 𝒲\mathcal{W}. In addition, Theorem 6 can also be perceived as a variation of Lemma 2 that bounds an nn-way divergence instead of TV-information. Finally, it is worth mentioning that one could also replace the nested applications of Doeblin curves in Theorem 6 or Lemma 2 with a product of power-constrained Doeblin coefficients to obtain a looser bound that remains meaningful for unbounded feasible sets if desired.

IV Proofs of Main Results on Doeblin Curves

In this section, we prove the main results presented in Section II, pertaining to fundamental properties of Doeblin coefficients and curves.

IV-A Proofs of Doeblin Characterizations

In this subsection, we first prove Propositions 1 and 2. Next, we introduce essential preliminaries (such as lattice infimum) required for generalizing the argument to Polish spaces. Finally, we present a detailed step-by-step proof of Theorem 1.

Proof of Proposition 1.

We have

τ(K)=(a)⋀x∈𝒳K(𝒴∣x)=(b)supℙ:Yx∼K(⋅∣x)ℙ(∀x,x′∈𝒳,Yx=Yx′),\tau(K)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(a)}}}{{=}}\bigwedge_{x\in\mathcal{X}}K(\mathcal{Y}\mid x)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(b)}}}{{=}}\!\!\sup_{\mathbb{P}:Y_{x}\sim K(\cdot\mid x)}\!\!\mathbb{P}\left(\forall x,x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X},\,Y_{x}=Y_{x^{\prime}}\right), (67)

where (a) holds by the greatest common component characterization of Doeblin coefficient Equation 11 and (b) holds by [19, Theorem 2], [47, Chapter 3, Theorem 7.3, p. 107]. ∎

We remark that for any kernel KK, the supremum in Equation 67 is achieved by the maximal coupling given by (cf. [19, Eq. 34], [47, Chapter 3, Theorem 7.3, p. 107])

∀x∈𝒳,Yx≜{Y∗,if I=1,Y~x,if I=0,\forall x\in\mathcal{X},\quad Y_{x}\triangleq\begin{cases}Y^{*},&\text{if $I=1$},\\ \tilde{Y}_{x},&\text{if $I=0$},\end{cases} (68)

where α=∧x∈𝒳K(𝒴∣x)\alpha=\wedge_{x\in\mathcal{X}}K(\mathcal{Y}\mid x) and the random variables II, Y∗Y^{*}, and {Y~x}x∈𝒳\{\tilde{Y}_{x}\}_{x\in\mathcal{X}} are sampled independently from the probability measures

I∼𝖡𝖾𝗋𝗇𝗈𝗎𝗅𝗅𝗂⁡(α),Y∗∼⋀x∈𝒳K(⋅∣x)α,\displaystyle I\sim\mathsf{Bernoulli}(\alpha),\quad Y^{*}\sim\frac{\bigwedge_{x\in\mathcal{X}}K({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid x)}{\alpha},
∀x∈𝒳,Y~x∼K(⋅∣x)−⋀x′∈𝒳K(⋅∣x′)1−α.\displaystyle\forall x\in\mathcal{X},\quad\tilde{Y}_{x}\sim\frac{K({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid x)-\bigwedge_{x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X}}K({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid x^{\prime})}{1-\alpha}.

(Note that Y∗Y^{*} and Y~x\tilde{Y}_{x} are unused in the case that their respective probability measures are undefined, i.e., α=0\alpha=0 or α=1\alpha=1.)
