Next, we present some preliminaries before carrying out the proof in the general setting of Polish spaces.

Definition 2 (Lattice Infimum [71, Section 2, p. 253]).

Let 𝒳\mathcal{X} be a Polish domain, and let ℱ\mathcal{F} be the set of all bounded measurable functions f:𝒳→ℝf\colon\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}. Given a measure μ:𝒳→ℝ+\mu\colon\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{+}, the lattice infimum of an arbitrary subset of functions 𝒢⊆ℱ\mathcal{G}\subseteq\mathcal{F}, denoted ∧~g∈𝒢g\ilatinf_{g\in\mathcal{G}}g, is the function in ℱ\mathcal{F} such that:

  1. 1.

    For each h∈𝒢h\in\mathcal{G},

    ⋀~g∈𝒢g≤h(μ-a.e.).\latinf_{g\in\mathcal{G}}g\leq h\quad\text{($\mu$-a.e.)}. (82)
  2. 2.

    For each f∈ℱf\in\mathcal{F}, if

    ∀h∈𝒢,(f≤h,(μ-a.e.)),\forall h\in\mathcal{G},\quad\Bigl(f\leq h\quad\text{($\mu$-a.e.)}\Bigr), (83)

    then

    f≤⋀~g∈𝒢g(μ-a.e.).f\leq\latinf_{g\in\mathcal{G}}g\quad\text{($\mu$-a.e.)}. (84)

For any 𝒢\mathcal{G}, the lattice infimum is μ\mu-a.e. unique. To see this, consider any two functions f1,f2∈ℱf_{1},f_{2}\in\mathcal{F} satisfying Definition 2. Since both functions satisfy the first condition Equation 82, both functions satisfy the antecedent in the second condition Equation 83, and so by the consequent in the second condition Equation 84, we have f1≤f2f_{1}\leq f_{2} (μ\mu-a.e.) and f2≤f1f_{2}\leq f_{1} (μ\mu-a.e.) Moreover, if 𝒢\mathcal{G} is countable, the lattice infimum is simply the pointwise infimum of functions in 𝒢\mathcal{G}, i.e., ∧~g∈𝒢g​(x)=inf{g⁡(x):g∈𝒢}\ilatinf_{g\in\mathcal{G}}g(x)=\inf\left\{g(x):g\in\mathcal{G}\right\}. However, when 𝒢\mathcal{G} is uncountable, the lattice infimum and pointwise infimum are different in general. We remark that the notion of lattice infimum serves primarily to avoid measurability issues, and the proof of Theorem 1 can be carried out without such notions for “well-behaved” kernels as shown in Appendix B for completeness.

The following lemma shows that the density of the greatest common component of a collection of measures is the lattice infimum of the individual measures’ densities.

Lemma 4 (Density of Greatest Common Component).

Let {πi}i∈ℐ\{\pi_{i}\}_{i\in\mathcal{I}} be a collection of measures on a Polish space (𝒴,ℱ𝒴)(\mathcal{Y},\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}}), where ℐ\mathcal{I} is an arbitrary index set. Assume each πi\pi_{i} is dominated by a common σ\sigma-finite measure μ\mu (i.e., πi≪μ\pi_{i}\ll\mu for all i∈ℐi\in\mathcal{I}). Then, we have the following properties.

  1. 1.

    The greatest common component ∧i∈ℐπi\wedge_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\pi_{i} is dominated by μ\mu, i.e., ∧i∈ℐπi≪μ\wedge_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\pi_{i}\ll\mu.

  2. 2.

    The lattice infimum ∧~i∈ℐd​πid​μ\ilatinf_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\frac{\mathrm{d}\pi_{i}}{\mathrm{d}\mu} exists.

  3. 3.

    The density of the greatest common component is dd​μ(∧i∈ℐπi)=∧~i∈ℐd​πid​μ\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\mu}(\wedge_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\pi_{i})=\ilatinf_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\frac{\mathrm{d}\pi_{i}}{\mathrm{d}\mu} (μ\mu-a.e.).

Proof.

Fix measures {πi}i∈ℐ\{\pi_{i}\}_{i\in\mathcal{I}} on (𝒴,ℱ𝒴)(\mathcal{Y},\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}}) satisfying πi≪μ\pi_{i}\ll\mu for each i∈ℐi\in\mathcal{I}.

Part 1: For any set A∈ℱ𝒴A\in\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}} with μ⁡(A)=0\mu(A)=0, we have

⋀i∈ℐπi​(A)≤(a)πi∗​(A)=(b)0\bigwedge_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\pi_{i}(A)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(a)}}}{{\leq}}\pi_{i^{*}}(A)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(b)}}}{{=}}0 (85)

as desired, where (a) holds for any i∗∈ℐi^{*}\in\mathcal{I} because the greatest common component of a collection of measures is a lower bound on each measure, and (b) holds because πi∗≪μ\pi_{i^{*}}\ll\mu.

Part 2: We refer readers to the analogous argument in [71, Lemma 2.6].

Part 3: For notational convenience, define a measure ν∗:ℱ𝒴→ℝ+\nu^{*}\colon\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{+} as

∀A∈ℱ𝒴,ν∗​(A)≜∫A(⋀~i∈ℐ⁡d​πi⁡d​μ)​⁡𝑑μ.\forall A\in\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}},\quad\nu^{*}(A)\triangleq\int_{A}\left(\latinf_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\frac{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\pi_{i}}{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu}\right)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu. (86)

First, observe that for any i∈ℐi\in\mathcal{I} and A∈ℱ𝒴A\in\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}}, we have

ν∗​(A)≤(a)∫A⁡d​πi⁡d​μ​⁡𝑑μ=(b)πi​(A),\displaystyle\nu^{*}(A)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(a)}}}{{\leq}}\int_{A}\frac{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\pi_{i}}{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(b)}}}{{=}}\pi_{i}(A), (87)

where (a) holds by Definition 2, Part 1 and (b) holds by definition of Radon-Nikodym derivative. Since ν∗≤πi\nu^{*}\leq\pi_{i} for each i∈ℐi\in\mathcal{I}, it follows that for each A∈ℱ𝒴A\in\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}},

ν∗(A)≤sup{ν(A):∀i∈ℐ,ν≤πi}.\nu^{*}(A)\leq\sup\left\{\nu(A):\forall i\in\mathcal{I},\,\nu\leq\pi_{i}\right\}. (88)

Next, observe that any measure ν\nu satisfying ν≤πi\nu\leq\pi_{i} for each i∈ℐi\in\mathcal{I} is itself dominated by μ\mu (i.e., ν≪μ\nu\ll\mu), because

ν⁡(A)≤πi​(A)=(a)0\nu(A)\leq\pi_{i}(A)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(a)}}}{{=}}0 (89)

for any set A∈ℱ𝒴A\in\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}} with μ⁡(A)=0\mu(A)=0, where (a) holds because πi≪μ\pi_{i}\ll\mu. Hence, by the Radon-Nikodym theorem, d​νd​μ\frac{\mathrm{d}\nu}{\mathrm{d}\mu} is well-defined. Moreover, we have

⁡d​ν⁡d​μ≤⁡d​πi⁡d​μ(μ-a.e.)\frac{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\nu}{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu}\leq\frac{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\pi_{i}}{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu}\quad\text{($\mu$-a.e.)} (90)

for each i∈ℐi\in\mathcal{I}. To see this, suppose the contrary: Assume that for some i∗∈ℐi^{*}\in\mathcal{I}, we have ⁡d​ν⁡d​μ>⁡d​πi∗⁡d​μ\frac{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\nu}{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu}>\frac{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\pi_{i^{*}}}{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu} on some set A∗∈ℱ𝒴A^{*}\in\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}} with μ⁡(A∗)>0\mu(A^{*})>0. Then,

ν⁡(A∗)=∫A∗⁡d​ν⁡d​μ​⁡𝑑μ>∫A∗⁡d​πi∗⁡d​μ​⁡𝑑μ=πi∗​(A∗),\nu(A^{*})=\int_{A^{*}}\frac{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\nu}{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu>\int_{A^{*}}\frac{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\pi_{i^{*}}}{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu=\pi_{i^{*}}(A^{*}), (91)

which contradicts the fact that ν≤πi∗\nu\leq\pi_{i^{*}}. Following from Equation 90, we have

⁡d​ν⁡d​μ≤⋀~i∈ℐ⁡d​πi⁡d​μ(μ-a.e.)\frac{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\nu}{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu}\leq\latinf_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\frac{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\pi_{i}}{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu}\quad\text{($\mu$-a.e.)} (92)

by Definition 2, Part 2, and therefore ν≤ν∗\nu\leq\nu^{*} by Equation 86. Since ν\nu was arbitrary, it follows that for each A∈ℱ𝒴A\in\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}},

ν∗(A)≥sup{ν(A):∀i∈ℐ,ν≤πi}.\displaystyle\nu^{*}(A)\geq\sup\left\{\nu(A):\forall i\in\mathcal{I},\,\nu\leq\pi_{i}\right\}. (93)

Proceeding onwards, for each A∈ℱ𝒴A\in\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}}, we have

∫A(⋀~i∈ℐ⁡d​πi⁡d​μ)dμ=(a)sup{ν(A):∀i∈ℐ,ν≤πi}=(b)⋀i∈ℐπi(A),\int_{A}\!\left(\latinf_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\frac{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\pi_{i}}{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu}\!\right)\!\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(a)}}}{{=}}\sup\left\{\nu(A):\forall i\in\mathcal{I},\,\nu\leq\pi_{i}\right\}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(b)}}}{{=}}\!\bigwedge_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\pi_{i}(A), (94)

where (a) holds by combining Equations 86, 93 and 88 and (b) holds by Equation 8. Hence, by definition of Radon-Nikodym derivative, dd​μ(∧i∈ℐπi)=∧~i∈ℐd​πid​μ\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\mu}(\wedge_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\pi_{i})=\ilatinf_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\frac{\mathrm{d}\pi_{i}}{\mathrm{d}\mu} as desired. ∎

Finally, we prove Theorem 1.

Proof of Theorem 1.

Fix an absolutely continuous Markov kernel K:𝒳×ℱ𝒴→[0,1]K\colon\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}}\rightarrow[0,1] with common dominating measure μ:ℱ𝒴→ℝ+\mu\colon\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{+}. We have

τ⁡(K)\displaystyle\tau(K) =(a)⋀x∈𝒳K⁡(𝒴∣x)\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(a)}}}{{=}}\bigwedge_{x\in\mathcal{X}}K(\mathcal{Y}\mid x) (95)
=(b)∫𝒴(⁡d⁡d​μ⋀x∈𝒳K(⋅∣x))dμ\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(b)}}}{{=}}\int_{\mathcal{Y}}\left(\frac{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}}{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu}\bigwedge_{x\in\mathcal{X}}K({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid x)\right)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu (96)
=(c)∫𝒴(⋀~x∈𝒳⁡dK⁡d​μ(⋅∣x))dμ,\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(c)}}}{{=}}\int_{\mathcal{Y}}\left(\latinf_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\frac{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}K}{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu}({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid x)\right)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu, (97)

where (a) holds by the greatest common component characterization of Doeblin coefficient Equation 11, (b) holds by definition of Radon-Nikodym derivative, and (c) holds by Lemma 4, Part 3.

Next, we compute the lattice infimum ∧~x∈𝒳dKd​μ(⋅∣x)\ilatinf_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\frac{\mathrm{d}K}{\mathrm{d}\mu}({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid x). For notational convenience, let

  ≜infn∈ℕinfx1,…,xn∈𝒳∫𝒴(mini∈[n]⁡d​K⁡d​μ(⋅∣xi))dμ.\displaystyle\hbox to9.93pt{\vbox to9.93pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\enskip\lower-4.9644pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke=#000000} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill=#000000} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width=0.4pt} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} {{{}}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} {{}{{{}}}{{}}{}{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{}{}{}{}{}{{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 6.59 0 C 6.59 3.64 3.64 6.59 0 6.59 C -3.64 6.59 -6.59 3.64 -6.59 0 C -6.59 -3.64 -3.64 -6.59 0 -6.59 C 3.64 -6.59 6.59 -3.64 6.59 0 Z M 0 0}{fill:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces }{{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@transformcm{1.0}{0.0}{0.0}{1.0}{-2.5pt}{-3.22221pt}\lxSVG@begingroup@{transform=matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 -3.46 -4.46)} \pgfsys@hbox{58}\lxSVG@closescope }}} \lxSVG@closescope }}} } \lxSVG@closescope {{{}}}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}\triangleq\inf_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\inf_{x_{1},\dots,x_{n}\in\mathcal{X}}\int_{\mathcal{Y}}\left(\min_{i\in[n]}\frac{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}K}{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu}({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid x_{i})\right)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu. (98)

For each k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, let sk≜{x^k,1,...,x^k,nk}⊆𝒳s_{k}\triangleq\{\hat{x}_{k,1},\mathinner{\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp\mkern-2.0mu\ldotp},\hat{x}_{k,n_{k}}\}\subseteq\mathcal{X} be a finite sequence such that

IV-B Proofs of Doeblin Curve Properties

In this subsection, we first prove Proposition 3. We begin by establishing two technical lemmata used in the proofs of Proposition 3 and subsequent results.

Lemma 5 (Doeblin Coefficients Under Affine Transformation).

Let W:𝒰×ℱ𝒳→[0,1]W\colon\mathcal{U}\times\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{X}}\rightarrow[0,1] and K:𝒳×ℱ𝒴→[0,1]K\colon\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}}\rightarrow[0,1] be Markov kernels. For any probability measures π,μ:ℱ𝒳→[0,1]\pi,\mu\colon\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{X}}\rightarrow[0,1] and scalars λ,α≥0\lambda,\alpha\geq 0 such that W−α​π≥0W-\alpha\pi\geq 0 and 1−λ​α¯≥01-\lambda\bar{\alpha}\geq 0 (where we define α¯≜1−α\bar{\alpha}\triangleq 1-\alpha for convenience), consider the Markov kernel W^:𝒰×ℱ𝒳→[0,1]\hat{W}\colon\mathcal{U}\times\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{X}}\rightarrow[0,1] given by W^=λ⁡(W−α​π)+(1−λ​α¯)​μ\hat{W}=\lambda\left(W-\alpha\pi\right)+\left(1-\lambda\bar{\alpha}\right)\mu. Then, the complementary Doeblin coefficients of W^\hat{W} and W^​K\hat{W}K are ρ⁡(W^)=λ​ρ​(W)\rho(\hat{W})=\lambda\,\rho(W) and ρ⁡(W^​K)=λ​ρ​(W​K)\rho(\hat{W}K)=\lambda\,\rho(WK).

Proof.

Fix Markov kernels WW and KK, probability measures π\pi and μ\mu, and scalars λ\lambda and α\alpha satisfying the conditions in Lemma 5. The complementary Doeblin coefficient of W^\hat{W} is

ρ⁡(W^)\displaystyle\phantom{{}={}}\rho(\hat{W}) (122)
=(a)1−⋀u∈𝒰W^​(𝒳∣u)\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(a)}}}{{=}}1-\bigwedge_{u\in\mathcal{U}}\hat{W}(\mathcal{X}\mid u) (123)
=(b)1−(λ⁡(⋀u∈𝒰W⁡(𝒳∣u)−α​π​(𝒳))+(1−λ​α¯)​μ​(𝒳))\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(b)}}}{{=}}1-\left(\lambda\left(\bigwedge_{u\in\mathcal{U}}W(\mathcal{X}\mid u)-\alpha\pi(\mathcal{X})\right)+\left(1-\lambda\bar{\alpha}\right)\mu(\mathcal{X})\right) (124)
=(c)1−(λ⁡(τ⁡(W)−α​π​(𝒳))+(1−λ​α¯)​μ​(𝒳))\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(c)}}}{{=}}1-\bigl(\lambda\left(\tau(W)-\alpha\pi(\mathcal{X})\right)+\left(1-\lambda\bar{\alpha}\right)\mu(\mathcal{X})\bigr) (125)
=(d)1−(λ⁡(τ⁡(W)−α)+(1−λ​α¯))\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(d)}}}{{=}}1-\bigl(\lambda\left(\tau(W)-\alpha\right)+\left(1-\lambda\bar{\alpha}\right)\bigr) (126)
=λ​ρ​(W)\displaystyle=\lambda\,\rho(W) (127)

as desired, where (a) and (c) hold by the greatest common component characterization of Doeblin coefficient Equation 11, (b) holds by Lemma 8, and (d) holds because π\pi and μ\mu are probability measures. The composition of W^\hat{W} with KK is

∀u∈𝒰,W^K(⋅∣u)=λ(WK(⋅∣u)−απK(⋅))+(1−λα¯)μK(⋅),\forall u\in\mathcal{U},\\ \hat{W}K({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid u)=\lambda\bigl(WK({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid u)-\alpha\pi K({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot\mkern 2.0mu})\bigr)+\left(1-\lambda\bar{\alpha}\right)\mu K({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot\mkern 2.0mu}),\ignorespaces\ignorespaces (128)

so the complementary Doeblin coefficient of W^​K\hat{W}K is

ρ⁡(W^​K)\displaystyle\rho(\hat{W}K) =(a)1−⋀u∈𝒰W^​K​(𝒴∣u)\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(a)}}}{{=}}1-\bigwedge_{u\in\mathcal{U}}\hat{W}K(\mathcal{Y}\mid u) (129)
=(b)1−(λ⁡(⋀u∈𝒰W​K​(𝒴∣u)−α​π​K​(𝒴))CLOSE\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(b)}}}{{=}}1-\Biggl(\lambda\left(\bigwedge_{u\in\mathcal{U}}WK(\mathcal{Y}\mid u)-\alpha\pi K(\mathcal{Y})\right) (130)
OPEN+(1−λ​α¯)​μ​K​(𝒴))\displaystyle\phantom{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(b)}}}{{=}}1-\Biggl(}+\left(1-\lambda\bar{\alpha}\right)\mu K(\mathcal{Y})\Biggr) (131)
=(c)1−(λ⁡(τ⁡(W​K)−α​π​K​(𝒴))+(1−λ​α¯)​μ​K​(𝒴))\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(c)}}}{{=}}1-\bigl(\lambda\left(\tau(WK)-\alpha\pi K(\mathcal{Y})\right)+\left(1-\lambda\bar{\alpha}\right)\mu K(\mathcal{Y})\bigr) (132)
=(d)1−(λ⁡(τ⁡(W​K)−α)+(1−λ​α¯))\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(d)}}}{{=}}1-\bigl(\lambda\left(\tau(WK)-\alpha\right)+\left(1-\lambda\bar{\alpha}\right)\bigr) (133)
=λ​ρ​(W​K)\displaystyle=\lambda\,\rho(WK) (134)

as desired, where (a) and (c) hold by the greatest common component characterization of Doeblin coefficient Equation 11, (b) holds by Lemmas 8 and , and (d) holds because π​K\pi K and μ​K\mu K are probability measures. ∎

Lemma 6 (Properties of Identity Kernel).

Let (𝒰,ℱ𝒰)(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{U}}) and (𝒳,ℱ𝒳)(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{X}}) be Polish spaces with 𝒰⊆𝒳\mathcal{U}\subseteq\mathcal{X}. Let K:𝒳×ℱ𝒴→[0,1]K\colon\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}}\rightarrow[0,1] be a Markov kernel. The identity kernel from 𝒰\mathcal{U} to 𝒳\mathcal{X}, i.e., Ξ:𝒰×ℱ𝒳→[0,1]\Xi\colon\mathcal{U}\times\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{X}}\rightarrow[0,1] where Ξ⁡(A∣u)=δu​(A)\Xi(A\mid u)=\updelta_{u}(A) for all u∈𝒰u\in\mathcal{U} and A∈ℱ𝒳A\in\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{X}}, satisfies ρ⁡(Ξ)=1\rho(\Xi)=1 and ρ​(Ξ​K)=ρ𝒰​(K)\rho(\Xi K)=\rho_{\mathcal{U}}(K).

Proof.

By inspection, the greatest common component of Ξ\Xi is ∧u∈𝒰Ξ(⋅∣u)=0\wedge_{u\in\mathcal{U}}\Xi({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid u)=0, and so the complementary Doeblin coefficient of Ξ\Xi, by Equation 11, is ρ(Ξ)=1−∧u∈𝒰Ξ(𝒳∣u)=1\rho(\Xi)=1-\wedge_{u\in\mathcal{U}}\Xi(\mathcal{X}\mid u)=1 as desired. By inspection, the composition of Ξ\Xi with KK is Ξ​K​(A∣u)=K⁡(A∣u)\Xi K(A\mid u)=K(A\mid u) for all u∈𝒰u\in\mathcal{U} and A∈ℱ𝒴A\in\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}}, and so the complementary Doeblin coefficient of Ξ​K\Xi K is ρ(ΞK)=1−∧u∈𝒰K(𝒴∣u)=ρ𝒰(K)\rho(\Xi K)=1-\wedge_{u\in\mathcal{U}}K(\mathcal{Y}\mid u)=\rho_{\mathcal{U}}(K) as desired. ∎

Now, we are ready to prove Proposition 3.

Proof of Proposition 3.

Part 1: Fix Markov kernels K1K_{1} and K2K_{2} and constraint sets 𝒢1\mathcal{G}_{1} and 𝒢2\mathcal{G}_{2}. We have

FK1​K2​(t,𝒢)\displaystyle\mathrm{F}_{K_{1}K_{2}}(t;\mathcal{G}) =(a)sup{ρ(WK1K2):ρ(W)≤t,W∈𝒢}\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(a)}}}{{=}}\sup\left\{\rho(WK_{1}K_{2})\!:\rho(W)\leq t,\,W\in\mathcal{G}\right\} (135)
≤(b)sup{ρ(VK2):ρ(V)≤FK1(t;𝒢1),V∈𝒢2}\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(b)}}}{{\leq}}\sup\left\{\rho(VK_{2}):\rho(V)\leq\mathrm{F}_{K_{1}}(t;\mathcal{G}_{1}),V\in\mathcal{G}_{2}\right\} (136)
=(c)FK2​(FK1​(t,𝒢1),𝒢2)\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(c)}}}{{=}}\mathrm{F}_{K_{2}}(\mathrm{F}_{K_{1}}(t;\mathcal{G}_{1});\mathcal{G}_{2}) (137)

as desired, where (a) and (c) hold by definition of Doeblin curve Equation 19, and (b) holds because any kernel W∈𝒢W\in\mathcal{G} with ρ⁡(W)≤t\rho(W)\leq t satisfies ρ(WK1)≤sup{ρ(WK1):ρ(W)≤t,W∈𝒢1}=FK1(t;𝒢1)\rho(WK_{1})\leq\sup\left\{\rho(WK_{1}):\rho(W)\leq t,\,W\in\mathcal{G}_{1}\right\}=\mathrm{F}_{K_{1}}(t;\mathcal{G}_{1}) and W​K1∈𝒢2WK_{1}\in\mathcal{G}_{2}.

Part 2: Fix a Markov kernel KK and a convex constraint set 𝒢\mathcal{G} containing the identity kernel Ξ(⋅∣u)=δu(⋅)\Xi({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid u)=\updelta_{u}({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot\mkern 2.0mu}) and a constant kernel W¯(⋅∣u)=π(⋅)\bar{W}({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid u)=\pi({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot\mkern 2.0mu}). For t=0t=0, we trivially have FK​(t,𝒢)=0=ρ⁡(K)​t\mathrm{F}_{K}(t;\mathcal{G})=0=\rho(K)\,t, so fix t∈(0,1]t\in(0,1] for the remainder of this part. Let W^:𝒳×ℱ𝒳→[0,1]\hat{W}\colon\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{X}}\rightarrow[0,1] be the Markov kernel given by W^(⋅∣u)≜tΞ(⋅∣u)+(1−t)W¯(⋅∣u)=tΞ(⋅∣u)+(1−t)π(⋅)\hat{W}({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid u)\triangleq t\,\Xi({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid u)+\left(1-t\right)\bar{W}({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid u)=t\,\Xi({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid u)+(1-t)\pi({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot\mkern 2.0mu}) for all u∈𝒳u\in\mathcal{X}. The complementary Doeblin coefficients of W^\hat{W} and W^​K\hat{W}K are

ρ⁡(W^)\displaystyle\rho(\hat{W}) =(a)t​ρ​(Ξ)=(b)t,\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(a)}}}{{=}}t\,\rho(\Xi)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(b)}}}{{=}}t, (138)
ρ⁡(W^​K)\displaystyle\rho(\hat{W}K) =(a)t​ρ​(Ξ​K)=(b)t​ρ𝒳​(K)=t​ρ​(K),\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(a)}}}{{=}}t\,\rho(\Xi K)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(b)}}}{{=}}t\,\rho_{\mathcal{X}}(K)=t\,\rho(K), (139)

where in each line (a) holds by Lemma 5 and (b) holds by Lemma 6. By convexity of 𝒢\mathcal{G}, we have W^∈𝒢\hat{W}\in\mathcal{G}. Hence,

FK​(t,𝒢)\displaystyle\mathrm{F}_{K}(t;\mathcal{G}) =(a)sup{ρ(WK):ρ(W)≤t,W∈𝒢}\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(a)}}}{{=}}\sup\left\{\rho(WK):\rho(W)\leq t,\,W\in\mathcal{G}\right\} (140)
≥ρ⁡(W^​K)=t​ρ​(K),\displaystyle\geq\rho(\hat{W}K)=t\,\rho(K), (141)

where (a) holds by definition of Doeblin curve Equation 19. Combining this lower bound with Equation 21 completes the proof.

Part 3: Fix a Markov kernel KK, a convex constraint set 𝒢\mathcal{G} containing a constant kernel W¯(⋅∣u)=π(⋅)\bar{W}({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid u)=\pi({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot\mkern 2.0mu}), and scalars λ∈[0,1]\lambda\in[0,1] and t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1]. Fix an arbitrary ϵ>0\epsilon>0. By definition of Doeblin curve as a supremum Equation 19, there exists a Markov kernel W∗∈𝒢W^{*}\in\mathcal{G} such that ρ⁡(W∗)≤t\rho(W^{*})\leq t and ρ⁡(W∗​K)≥FK​(t,𝒢)−ϵ\rho(W^{*}K)\geq\mathrm{F}_{K}(t;\mathcal{G})-\epsilon. Define another Markov kernel W^\hat{W} as W^(⋅∣u)≜λW∗(⋅∣u)+(1−λ)W¯(⋅∣u)=λW∗(⋅∣u)+(1−λ)π(⋅)\hat{W}({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid u)\triangleq\lambda W^{*}({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid u)+\left(1-\lambda\right)\bar{W}({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid u)=\lambda W^{*}({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid u)+\left(1-\lambda\right)\pi({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot\mkern 2.0mu}) for all u∈𝒰u\in\mathcal{U}. By Lemma 5, we have ρ⁡(W^)=λ​ρ​(W∗)≤λ​t\rho(\hat{W})=\lambda\,\rho(W^{*})\leq\lambda t and ρ⁡(W^​K)=λ​ρ​(W∗​K)≥λ⁡(FK​(t,𝒢)−ϵ)\rho(\hat{W}K)=\lambda\,\rho(W^{*}K)\geq\lambda\left(\mathrm{F}_{K}(t;\mathcal{G})-\epsilon\right). By convexity of 𝒢\mathcal{G}, we have W^∈𝒢\hat{W}\in\mathcal{G}. Hence,

FK​(λ​t,𝒢)\displaystyle\mathrm{F}_{K}(\lambda t;\mathcal{G}) =(a)sup{ρ(WK):ρ(W)≤λt,W∈𝒢}\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(a)}}}{{=}}\sup\left\{\rho(WK):\rho(W)\leq\lambda t,\,W\in\mathcal{G}\right\} (142)
≥ρ⁡(W^​K)\displaystyle\geq\rho(\hat{W}K) (143)
≥λ⁡(FK​(t,𝒢)−ϵ),\displaystyle\geq\lambda\left(\mathrm{F}_{K}(t;\mathcal{G})-\epsilon\right), (144)

where (a) holds by definition of Doeblin curve Equation 19. Since ϵ>0\epsilon>0 was arbitrary, we have FK​(λ​t,𝒢)≥λ​FK​(t,𝒢)\mathrm{F}_{K}(\lambda t;\mathcal{G})\geq\lambda\mathrm{F}_{K}(t;\mathcal{G}) as desired.

Finally, to show the equivalent characterization that t↦FK​(t,𝒢)/tt\mapsto\mathrm{F}_{K}(t;\mathcal{G})/t is non-increasing, fix s,t∈(0,1]s,t\in(0,1] such that s<ts<t and observe that

FK​(s,𝒢)s≥(a)(st)​FK​(t,𝒢)s=FK​(t,𝒢)t,\frac{\mathrm{F}_{K}(s;\mathcal{G})}{s}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(a)}}}{{\geq}}\left(\frac{s}{t}\right)\frac{\mathrm{F}_{K}(t;\mathcal{G})}{s}=\frac{\mathrm{F}_{K}(t;\mathcal{G})}{t}, (145)

where (a) holds by applying Equation 144 with λ≜s/t<1\lambda\triangleq s/t<1.

Part 4: By definition of Lipschitz continuity, we want to show that |FK​(s,𝒢)−FK​(t,𝒢)|≤|s−t|\left\lvert\mathrm{F}_{K}(s;\mathcal{G})-\mathrm{F}_{K}(t;\mathcal{G})\right\rvert\leq\left\lvert s-t\right\rvert for all s,t∈[0,1]s,t\in[0,1]. Fix s,t∈[0,1]s,t\in[0,1] such that s<ts<t. If s=0s=0, the result trivially follows from Equation 22. Otherwise, we have

|FK​(s,𝒢)−FK​(t,𝒢)|\displaystyle\left\lvert\mathrm{F}_{K}(s;\mathcal{G})-\mathrm{F}_{K}(t;\mathcal{G})\right\rvert =(a)ts​(st)​FK​(t,𝒢)−FK​(s,𝒢)\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(a)}}}{{=}}\frac{t}{s}\left(\frac{s}{t}\right)\mathrm{F}_{K}(t;\mathcal{G})-\mathrm{F}_{K}(s;\mathcal{G}) (146)
≤(b)ts​FK​(s,𝒢)−FK​(s,𝒢)\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(b)}}}{{\leq}}\frac{t}{s}\,\mathrm{F}_{K}(s;\mathcal{G})-\mathrm{F}_{K}(s;\mathcal{G}) (147)
=(t−s)​FK​(s,𝒢)s\displaystyle=(t-s)\,\frac{\mathrm{F}_{K}(s;\mathcal{G})}{s} (148)
≤(c)t−s\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(c)}}}{{\leq}}t-s (149)
=(d)|s−t|\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(d)}}}{{=}}\left\lvert s-t\right\rvert (150)

as desired, where (a) holds because FK​(s,𝒢)≤FK​(t,𝒢)\mathrm{F}_{K}(s;\mathcal{G})\leq\mathrm{F}_{K}(t;\mathcal{G}) by monotonicity of Doeblin curves, (b) holds by applying Part 3 with λ≜s/t<1\lambda\triangleq s/t<1, (c) holds because FK​(s)≤s\mathrm{F}_{K}(s)\leq s by Equation 22, and (d) holds because s<ts<t. ∎

Next, we prove Proposition 4.

Proof of Proposition 5.

Fix a Markov kernel K:𝒳×ℱ𝒴→[0,1]K\colon\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}}\rightarrow[0,1]. Fix scalars t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1], p∈[0,∞)p\in[0,\infty), and λ>0\lambda>0 such that λ​t≤1\lambda t\leq 1.1313 13 The proposition trivially holds for λ=0\lambda=0, so we assume λ>0\lambda>0 throughout this proof. We will consider two cases.

Case 1: λ≤1\lambda\leq 1. We follow the argument from [25, Proposition 2]. First, we will show that

FK​(λ​t,λ​p)≥λ​FK​(t,p).\mathrm{F}_{K}(\lambda t;\lambda p)\geq\lambda\mathrm{F}_{K}(t;p). (203)

Fix any arbitrary ϵ>0\epsilon>0. By definition of Doeblin curve, there exists a Markov kernel W∗:𝒰×ℱ𝒳→[0,1]W^{*}\colon\mathcal{U}\times\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{X}}\rightarrow[0,1] such that ρ⁡(W∗)≤t\rho(W^{*})\leq t, |||W∗|||≤p|\mathchoice{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-2.5mu}{}\mathinner{|\mathchoice{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-2.5mu}{}\mathinner{|W^{*}|}\mathchoice{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-2.5mu}{}|}\mathchoice{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-2.5mu}{}|\leq p, and ρ⁡(W∗​K)≥FK​(t,p)−ϵ\rho(W^{*}K)\geq\mathrm{F}_{K}(t;p)-\epsilon. |||W^|||\displaystyle|\mathchoice{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-2.5mu}{}\mathinner{|\mathchoice{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-2.5mu}{}\mathinner{|\hat{W}|}\mathchoice{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-2.5mu}{}|}\mathchoice{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-2.5mu}{}| =λ⁡⦀W∗⦀≤λ​p.\displaystyle=\lambda\left|\mathchoice{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-2.5mu}{}\left|\mathchoice{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-2.5mu}{}\left|W^{*}\right|\mathchoice{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-2.5mu}{}\right|\mathchoice{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-2.5mu}{}\right|\leq\lambda p. ≥(b)ρ⁡(W^​K)≥(c)λ⁡(FK​(t,p)−ϵ),\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(b)}}}{{\geq}}\rho(\hat{W}K)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(c)}}}{{\geq}}\lambda\left(\mathrm{F}_{K}(t;p)-\epsilon\right), (208)

where (a) holds by definition of Doeblin curve, (b) holds by Equations 204 and 206, and (c) holds by Equation 205. Since ϵ>0\epsilon>0 was arbitrary, this shows Equation 203 as desired.

Fix any arbitrary ϵ>0\epsilon>0. By definition of Doeblin curve, there exists a Markov kernel W∗:𝒰×ℱ𝒳→[0,1]W^{*}\colon\mathcal{U}\times\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{X}}\rightarrow[0,1] such that ρ⁡(W∗)≤λ​t\rho(W^{*})\leq\lambda t, ‖|W∗|‖≤λ​p\left|\mathchoice{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-2.5mu}{}\left|\mathchoice{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-2.5mu}{}\left|W^{*}\right|\mathchoice{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-2.5mu}{}\right|\mathchoice{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-4.5mu}{{}\mkern-2.5mu}{}\right|\leq\lambda p, and ρ⁡(W∗​K)≥FK​(λ​t,λ​p)−ϵ\rho(W^{*}K)\geq\mathrm{F}_{K}(\lambda t;\lambda p)-\epsilon. V Proofs of Main Results on Applications

In this section, we prove the main results presented in Section III, pertaining to applications of Doeblin curves.

Now, we are ready to prove Theorem 4.

Proof of Theorem 4.

Define a function f:[0,1]→[0,1]f\colon[0,1]\rightarrow[0,1] as f⁡(t)≜FinvbreveΦ𝖴𝖠​(min⁡{1,b​t},p)f(t)\triangleq\invbreve{\mathrm{F}}_{\Phi}^{\mathsf{UA}}\left(\min\left\{1,bt\right\};p\right). Also, 1≥f⁡(1)1\geq f(1) by the range of ff. Hence, applying Kleene’s fixed point theorem [75] on ([0,1],≥)([0,1],\geq),

lims→∞f(s)​(1)=(a)infs∈ℕf(s)​(1)=max⁡{t∈[0,1]:f⁡(t)=t},\lim_{s\rightarrow\infty}f^{(s)}(1)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(a)}}}{{=}}\inf_{s\in\mathbb{N}}{f^{(s)}(1)}=\max\left\{t\in[0,1]:f(t)=t\right\}, (389)

where f(s)f^{(s)} denotes the ss-fold composition of ff, and (a) holds because f(s)​(1)f^{(s)}(1) is monotonically non-increasing in ss.

With this groundwork established, we commence our main argument. Fix ϵ>0\epsilon>0, and fix nn sufficiently large such that for all s≥⌈logb⁡(n)⌉s\geq\lceil\log_{b}(n)\rceil,

f(s)​(1)≤max⁡{t∈[0,1]:f⁡(t)=t}+ϵ.f^{(s)}(1)\leq\max\left\{t\in[0,1]:f(t)=t\right\}+\epsilon. (390)

Consider any nn-input circuit of noisy gates where each gate has at most bb inputs. Define the height of an input vertex XiX_{i} as the length of the shortest directed path from XiX_{i} to the output vertex YmY_{m}, where the existence of such a path is guaranteed for each XiX_{i} by the formal model defined in Section III-B. Since the in-degree of each gate vertex is at most bb, there must exist at least one input vertex whose height is ⌈logb⁡(n)⌉\lceil\log_{b}(n)\rceil or greater.1919 19 To see this, consider all circuits where the in-degree of each gate is at most bb and the height of each input vertex is at most hmax≜⌈logb⁡(n)−1⌉h_{\max}\triangleq\lceil\log_{b}(n)-1\rceil, and let CC be such a circuit with the greatest number of input vertices. We may assume that no vertex in CC has multiple outgoing edges, since we may equivalently consider the tree generated by running breadth-first traversal starting from YmY_{m} and following edges in reverse direction, which preserves the heights of all input vertices. Furthermore, each gate vertex in CC must have exactly bb incoming edges; otherwise, additional input vertices may be added to the gate and hence to CC. Lastly, each vertex in CC with height less than hmaxh_{\max} must be a gate, since if such a vertex was an input, replacing it with a gate taking bb new input vertices would add b−1b-1 input vertices to CC overall. Hence, CC is a perfect bb-ary anti-arborescence where all input vertices have height hmaxh_{\max}, and so CC has bhmax<blogb⁡(n)=nb^{h_{\max}}<b^{\log_{b}(n)}=n inputs. Without loss of generality, let X1X_{1} be such an input vertex.

VI Conclusion

In closing, we review our main contributions and propose some directions for follow-up work. In this paper, we formulated the notion of a Doeblin curve to quantify information contraction of Markov kernels on collections of arbitrarily many input distributions with specific divergence and power levels, building upon existing literature on Doeblin coefficients and nonlinear information contraction. After introducing a new variational characterization of Doeblin coefficients, we established several properties of Doeblin curves and derived bounds on Doeblin curves under canonical power constraints and regularity conditions. With this more nuanced measure of information contraction in place, we presented three theoretical applications in noisy iterative optimization, reliable computation, and differential privacy, leveraging Doeblin curves to generalize results in these areas to multi-way or unbounded settings where Doeblin coefficients fail to capture information contraction.

We suggest two potential extensions of our present work. Firstly, our current understanding of Doeblin curves may be further enriched by establishing precise conditions for concavity and by studying examples of closed-form uniform average Doeblin curves. Secondly, future research may explore and broaden our proposed definition of group local differential privacy Equation 52, since the standard definition of differential privacy is sometimes considered very stringent for many applications [76, 77].

Appendix A Technical Lemmata

In this appendix, we state and prove two miscellaneous results used throughout our paper.

Lemma 8 (Greatest Common Component Under Affine Transformation).

For any kernel W:𝒰×ℱ𝒳→ℝ+W\colon\mathcal{U}\times\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{X}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{+} and signed measure π:ℱ𝒳→ℝ\pi\colon\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{X}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}, the greatest common component of the kernel W^:𝒰×ℱ𝒳→ℝ+\hat{W}\colon\mathcal{U}\times\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{X}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{+} given by

∀u∈𝒰,W^(⋅∣u)≜αW(⋅∣u)+π(⋅),\forall u\in\mathcal{U},\quad\hat{W}({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid u)\triangleq\alpha W({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid u)+\pi({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot\mkern 2.0mu}), (505)

where α≥0\alpha\geq 0 and π\pi are such that W^≥0\hat{W}\geq 0, is

⋀u∈𝒰W^(⋅∣u)=α⋀u∈𝒰W(⋅∣u)+π(⋅).\bigwedge_{u\in\mathcal{U}}\hat{W}({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid u)=\alpha\bigwedge_{u\in\mathcal{U}}W({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid u)+\pi({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot\mkern 2.0mu}). (506)
Proof.

The lemma trivially holds for α=0\alpha=0, so assume α>0\alpha>0 henceforth. For notational convenience, let μ∗\mu^{*} denote the measure given by the right-hand side of Equation 506. By definition of greatest common component as a supremum in Equation 8, we seek to verify two properties of μ∗\mu^{*}.

Firstly, μ∗\mu^{*} satisfies the condition of the supremum W^≥μ∗\hat{W}\geq\mu^{*}, because for any u∈𝒰u\in\mathcal{U},

W^(⋅∣u)=(a)αW(⋅∣u)+π(⋅)≥(b)α⋀u∈𝒰W(⋅∣u)+π(⋅)=(c)μ∗(⋅),\hat{W}({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid u)\!\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(a)}}}{{=}}\!\alpha W({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid u)+\pi({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot\mkern 2.0mu})\!\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(b)}}}{{\geq}}\!\alpha\!\bigwedge_{u\in\mathcal{U}}\!W({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid u)+\pi({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot\mkern 2.0mu})\!\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(c)}}}{{=}}\!\mu^{*}({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot\mkern 2.0mu}), (507)

where (a) holds by definition of W^\hat{W} Equation 505, (b) holds because the greatest common component of a kernel is a lower bound on the kernel, and (c) holds by definition of μ∗\mu^{*} as the right-hand side of Equation 506.

Secondly, we will prove that for any measure μ\mu satisfying W^≥μ\hat{W}\geq\mu, we have μ∗≥μ\mu^{*}\geq\mu. Fix a measure μ\mu such that W^≥μ\hat{W}\geq\mu. Observe that

∀u∈𝒰,W(⋅∣u)=(a)W^(⋅∣u)−π(⋅)α≥μ⁡(⋅)−π⁡(⋅)α,\forall u\in\mathcal{U},\quad W({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid u)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(a)}}{{=}}\frac{\hat{W}({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid u)-\pi({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot\mkern 2.0mu})}{\alpha}\geq\frac{\mu({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot\mkern 2.0mu})-\pi({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot\mkern 2.0mu})}{\alpha}, (508)

where (a) holds by rearranging Equation 505. Consider a Hahn-Jordan decomposition of μ−π\mu-\pi, i.e.,

∀A∈ℱ𝒳,(μ−π)+​(A)≜(μ−π)​(A∩P),(μ−π)−​(A)≜−(μ−π)​(A∩N),\forall A\in\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{X}},\quad\begin{aligned} \left(\mu-\pi\right)^{+}(A)&\triangleq\left(\mu-\pi\right)(A\cap P),\\ \left(\mu-\pi\right)^{-}(A)&\triangleq-\left(\mu-\pi\right)(A\cap N),\end{aligned} (509)

where P⊆𝒳P\subseteq\mathcal{X} and N=PcN=P^{\mathrm{c}} are the supports (modulo null sets) of the positive and negative parts of μ−π\mu-\pi, respectively. Then,

W⁡(A∣u)\displaystyle W(A\mid u) =(a)W⁡(A∩P∣u)+W⁡(A∩N∣u)\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(a)}}}{{=}}W(A\cap P\mid u)+W(A\cap N\mid u) (510)
≥(b)(μ−π)​(A∩P)α+0\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(b)}}}{{\geq}}\frac{\left(\mu-\pi\right)(A\cap P)}{\alpha}+0 (511)
=(c)(μ−π)+​(A)α\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(c)}}}{{=}}\frac{\left(\mu-\pi\right)^{+}(A)}{\alpha} (512)

Lemma 9 (Properties of Upper Concave Envelope).

Let f:ℐ→[0,1]f\colon\mathcal{I}\rightarrow[0,1] be a function defined on a (possibly infinite) interval ℐ⊆ℝ+\mathcal{I}\subseteq\mathbb{R}_{+}. The upper concave envelope f𝑖𝑛𝑣𝑏𝑟𝑒𝑣𝑒:ℐ→[0,1]\invbreve{f}\colon\mathcal{I}\rightarrow[0,1] of ff satisfies the following properties:

  1. 1.

    For all boundary points tt of ℐ\mathcal{I}, we have finvbreve​(t)=f​(t)\invbreve{f}(t)=f(t).

  2. 2.

    If ff is non-decreasing, then finvbreve\invbreve{f} is non-decreasing.

  3. 3.

    If ff is non-decreasing, ℐ=[0,1]\mathcal{I}=[0,1], and f⁡(t)≤tf(t)\leq t for all t∈ℐt\in\mathcal{I}, then finvbreve\invbreve{f} is continuous on ℐ\mathcal{I}.

Proof.

Part 1: Consider a boundary point a∈ℐa\in\mathcal{I}. Suppose for the sake of contradiction that finvbreve​(a)≠f​(a)\invbreve{f}(a)\neq f(a). Since finvbreve≥f\invbreve{f}\geq f everywhere on ℐ\mathcal{I} by definition of upper concave envelope, we must have finvbreve​(a)>f​(a)\invbreve{f}(a)>f(a). Consider the function g:ℐ→[0,1]g\colon\mathcal{I}\rightarrow[0,1] given by

∀t∈ℐ,g⁡(t)≜{f⁡(a),if t=a,finvbreve​(t),if t≠a.\forall t\in\mathcal{I},\quad g(t)\triangleq\begin{cases}f(a),&\text{if $t=a$},\\ \invbreve{f}(t),&\text{if $t\neq a$}.\end{cases} (514)

Clearly, f≤g≤finvbrevef\leq g\leq\invbreve{f} everywhere on ℐ\mathcal{I}. Moreover, gg is concave, because for all distinct s,t∈ℐs,t\in\mathcal{I} and all θ∈(0,1)\theta\in(0,1),

g⁡(θ​s+(1−θ)​t)\displaystyle g(\theta s+\left(1-\theta\right)t) =(a)finvbreve​(θ​s+(1−θ)​t)≥(b)θ​finvbreve​(s)+(1−θ)​finvbreve​(t)\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(a)}}}{{=}}\invbreve{f}(\theta s+\left(1-\theta\right)t)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(b)}}}{{\geq}}\theta\,\invbreve{f}(s)+\left(1-\theta\right)\invbreve{f}(t) (515)
≥(c)θ​g​(s)+(1−θ)​g​(t),\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(c)}}}{{\geq}}\theta\,g(s)+\left(1-\theta\right)g(t), (516)

where (a) holds by the second case in Equation 514 because θ​s+(1−θ)​t\theta s+(1-\theta)t is an interior point of ℐ\mathcal{I}, (b) holds because finvbreve\invbreve{f} is concave, and (c) holds because g≤finvbreveg\leq\invbreve{f} everywhere, as mentioned above. This contradicts the fact that finvbreve\invbreve{f} is the pointwise infimum of all concave upper bounds of ff.

Part 2: Let f¯:ℐ→ℝ\bar{f}:\mathcal{I}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} be the closed upper concave envelope (or “closed convex hull”) of ff [44, Chapter B, Proposition 2.5.2, Definition 2.5.3], i.e.,

∀t∈ℐ,f¯(t)≜inf{αt+β:α≥0,β∈ℝ such that ∀s∈ℐ,αs+β≥f(s)},\forall t\in\mathcal{I},\kern 5.0pt\bar{f}(t)\triangleq\inf\{\alpha t+\beta:\alpha\geq 0,\,\beta\in\mathbb{R}\text{ such that }\\ \forall s\in\mathcal{I},\,\alpha s+\beta\geq f(s)\},\ignorespaces\ignorespaces (517)

where it suffices to consider only α≥0\alpha\geq 0 because ff is non-decreasing. Fix s,t∈ℐs,t\in\mathcal{I} such that s<ts<t. By definition of f¯\bar{f} as an infimum , there exist sequences of coefficients {αn}n∈ℕ⊂ℝ+\{\alpha_{n}\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\subset\mathbb{R}_{+} and {βn}n∈ℕ⊂ℝ\{\beta_{n}\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\subset\mathbb{R}, satisfying αn​s+βn≥f⁡(s)\alpha_{n}s+\beta_{n}\geq f(s) for all s∈ℐs\in\mathcal{I} and n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, such that f¯​(t)=limn→∞{αn​t+βn}\bar{f}(t)=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\{\alpha_{n}t+\beta_{n}\}. It follows that

f¯​(s)\displaystyle\bar{f}(s) ≤(a)infn∈ℕ{αn​s+βn}≤limn→∞{αn​s+βn}\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(a)}}}{{\leq}}\inf_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\left\{\alpha_{n}s+\beta_{n}\right\}\leq\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\left\{\alpha_{n}s+\beta_{n}\right\} (518)
≤(b)limn→∞{αn​t+βn}=f¯​(t),\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(b)}}}{{\leq}}\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\left\{\alpha_{n}t+\beta_{n}\right\}=\bar{f}(t), (519)

where (a) holds by taking the infimum in over a smaller set, and (b) holds because s<ts<t and αn≥0\alpha_{n}\geq 0 for all n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}. This establishes that f¯\bar{f} is non-decreasing on ℐ\mathcal{I}. Since f¯\bar{f} is the closure of finvbreve\invbreve{f} [44, Chapter B, Proposition 2.5.2], f¯\bar{f} and finvbreve\invbreve{f} agree on the interior of ℐ\mathcal{I} [44, Chapter B, Proposition 1.2.6] and finvbreve≤f¯\invbreve{f}\leq\bar{f} on any boundary points of ℐ\mathcal{I}. Hence, finvbreve\invbreve{f} is non-decreasing on ℐ−{supℐ}\mathcal{I}-\{\sup\mathcal{I}\}. If ℐ\mathcal{I} is finite and includes its right boundary point b∈ℐb\in\mathcal{I}, then finvbreve​(b)≤f¯​(b)≤f⁡(b)\invbreve{f}(b)\leq\bar{f}(b)\leq f(b), where the second inequality holds by upper-bounding the infimum in with the specific majorant α=0\alpha=0 and β=f⁡(b)\beta=f(b). By Part 1, finvbreve​(b)=f​(b)\invbreve{f}(b)=f(b), and so finvbreve​(b)=f¯​(b)\invbreve{f}(b)=\bar{f}(b). Thus, finvbreve\invbreve{f} is non-decreasing on all of ℐ\mathcal{I}, as desired.

Part 3: By concavity, finvbreve\invbreve{f} is continuous on the interior of ℐ\mathcal{I}. To establish the continuity of finvbreve\invbreve{f} at 00, observe that

∀t∈ℐ,finvbreve​(t)≥(a)finvbreve​(0)=(b)f⁡(0)=(c)0,\forall t\in\mathcal{I},\kern 5.0pt\invbreve{f}(t)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(a)}}}{{\geq}}\invbreve{f}(0)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(b)}}}{{=}}f(0)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(c)}}}{{=}}0, (520)

where (a) holds by Part 2, (b) holds by Part 1, and (c) holds by the assumption f⁡(t)≤tf(t)\leq t and the range of ff. Furthermore,

∀t∈ℐ,finvbreve​(t)≤f¯​(t)≤(a)t,\forall t\in\mathcal{I},\kern 5.0pt\invbreve{f}(t)\leq\bar{f}(t)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(a)}}}{{\leq}}t, (521)

where (a) holds by upper-bounding the infimum in with the specific majorant α=1\alpha=1 and β=0\beta=0 due to the assumption f⁡(t)≤tf(t)\leq t. Hence, we have limt→0+finvbreve​(t)=0=finvbreve​(0)\lim_{t\rightarrow 0^{+}}\invbreve{f}(t)=0=\invbreve{f}(0) as desired. To establish the continuity of finvbreve\invbreve{f} at 11, observe that limt→1−finvbreve​(t)≤finvbreve​(1)\lim_{t\rightarrow 1^{-}}\invbreve{f}(t)\leq\invbreve{f}(1) because finvbreve\invbreve{f} is non-decreasing by Part 2, and limt→1−finvbreve​(t)≥limt→1−{t​finvbreve​(1)+(1−t)​finvbreve​(0)}=finvbreve​(1)\lim_{t\rightarrow 1^{-}}\invbreve{f}(t)\geq\lim_{t\rightarrow 1^{-}}\{t\,\invbreve{f}(1)+\left(1-t\right)\invbreve{f}(0)\}=\invbreve{f}(1) because finvbreve\invbreve{f} is concave. Hence, limt→1−finvbreve​(t)=finvbreve​(1)\lim_{t\rightarrow 1^{-}}\invbreve{f}(t)=\invbreve{f}(1) as desired. ∎

Appendix B Variational Characterization Under Equicontinuity

In this appendix, we provide an alternative statement and proof of Theorem 1 without the use of lattice infima, under the assumption of equicontinuity of the kernel KK.

Theorem 7 (Variational Characterization of Doeblin Coefficient).

Let (𝒳,d𝒳)(\mathcal{X},d_{\mathcal{X}}) and (𝒴,ℱ𝒴)(\mathcal{Y},\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}}) be Polish spaces, where 𝒳\mathcal{X} is endowed with the metric d𝒳:𝒳×𝒳→ℝ+d_{\mathcal{X}}\colon\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{+}. Let K:𝒳×ℱ𝒴→[0,1]K\colon\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}}\rightarrow[0,1] be an absolutely continuous Markov kernel with respect to the σ\sigma-finite measure μ:ℱ𝒴→ℝ+\mu\colon\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{+}. Assume the family of functions {x↦d​Kd​μ​(y∣x):y∈𝒴}\{x\mapsto\frac{\mathrm{d}K}{\mathrm{d}\mu}(y\mid x):y\in\mathcal{Y}\} is equicontinuous [78, Definition 7.22], i.e.,

∀ϵ>0,∃δ>0,∀x,x′∈𝒳,∀y∈𝒴,d𝒳​(x,x′)<δ⟹|⁡d​K⁡d​μ​(y∣x)−⁡d​K⁡d​μ​(y∣x′)|<ϵ.\forall\epsilon>0,\,\exists\delta>0,\,\forall x,x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X},\,\forall y\in\mathcal{Y},\\ d_{\mathcal{X}}(x,x^{\prime})<\delta\implies\left\lvert\frac{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}K}{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu}(y\mid x)-\frac{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}K}{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu}(y\mid x^{\prime})\right\rvert<\epsilon.\ignorespaces\ignorespaces (522)

We remark that the equicontinuity assumption on KK allows us to circumvent measurability issues in the proof by defining gg as the pointwise infimum over a countable dense subset of 𝒳\mathcal{X}, which is guaranteed to be measurable while approximating the infimum over all of general uncountable 𝒳\mathcal{X} to any ϵ>0\epsilon>0 accuracy. Otherwise, gg would have to be defined as the lattice or essential infimum, as was done in the proof of Theorem 1 in Section IV-A.

Appendix C Markov Kernel Examples

In this appendix, we provide examples of non-trivial Markov kernels satisfying the preconditions for various results in our paper. Throughout this appendix, let Φ:ℝ→(0,1)\Phi\colon\mathbb{R}\rightarrow(0,1) denote the standard Gaussian CDF Φ(x)≜∫−∞x(1/2​π)exp(−t2/2)dt\Phi(x)\triangleq\int_{-\infty}^{x}(1/\sqrt{2\pi})\exp(-t^{2}/2)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t.

First, we present a Markov kernel W:𝒰×ℱ𝒳→[0,1]W\colon\mathcal{U}\times\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{X}}\rightarrow[0,1] with a countably infinite source space 𝒰\mathcal{U}, unbounded support on the target space 𝒳\mathcal{X}, and finite average extremal power.

Proposition 10 (Average Extremal Power Example).

where c>0c>0 is a fixed constant. Next, we present a Markov kernel W:𝒰×ℱ𝒳→[0,1]W\colon\mathcal{U}\times\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{X}}\rightarrow[0,1] with an uncountable source space 𝒰\mathcal{U}, unbounded support on the target space 𝒳\mathcal{X}, and finite average extremal power.

Proposition 11 (Average Extremal Power Example).

Let 𝒰≜(0,∞)\mathcal{U}\triangleq(0,\infty) and 𝒳≜ℝ\mathcal{X}\triangleq\mathbb{R}. Let W:𝒰×ℱ𝒳→[0,1]W\colon\mathcal{U}\times\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{X}}\rightarrow[0,1] be the Markov kernel such that for each u∈𝒰u\in\mathcal{U}, Xu∼W(⋅∣u)X_{u}\sim W({\mkern 2.0mu\cdot}\mid u) is given by

Xu∼{𝖭𝗈𝗋𝗆𝖺𝗅⁡(0,1),if Ju=1,2​𝖡𝖾𝗍𝖺​(u,u)−1,if Ju=0,X_{u}\sim\begin{cases}\mathsf{Normal}\left(0,1\right),&\text{if $J_{u}=1$},\\ 2\,\mathsf{Beta}(u,u)-1,&\text{if $J_{u}=0$},\end{cases} (553)

=a2+ς22.\displaystyle=\frac{a^{2}+\varsigma^{2}}{2}. (623)

Hence, the pre-image of any measurable set A⊆ℝ{A\subseteq\mathbb{R}} under supu∈𝒰{Zu−𝔼⁡[Zu]}\sup_{u\in\mathcal{U}}\{Z_{u}-\mathbb{E}\left[Z_{u}\right]\} is the measurable event ({I=1}∩{X∗∈𝒮A})∪{I=0}(\{I=1\}\cap\{X^{*}\in\mathcal{S}_{A}\})\allowbreak\cup\{I=0\} if (a2+ς2)/2∈A(a^{2}+\varsigma^{2})/2\in A, and the measurable event {I=1}∩{X∗∈𝒮A}\left\{I=1\right\}\cap\{X^{*}\in\mathcal{S}_{A}\} otherwise, where 𝒮A⊆ℝ\mathcal{S}_{A}\subseteq\mathbb{R} is the set 𝒮A={−z+ς2/2,z+ς2/2:z∈A,z≥−ς2/2}\mathcal{S}_{A}=\{-\sqrt{z+\varsigma^{2}/2},\sqrt{z+\varsigma^{2}/2}:z\in A,\,z\geq-\varsigma^{2}/2\}. ∎

Appendix D Doeblin Curves and Markov Chains

Lastly, we conclude with a discussion relating Doeblin curves back to the classic setting of Markov chain ergodicity. As a minor departure from our previous exclusive focus on Doeblin curves, we will also discuss contraction properties of Doeblin coefficients here. Throughout this appendix, we focus on the special case of discrete-time finite-state time-homogeneous Markov chains, which we represent as a row stochastic matrix 𝐊∈ℝ𝗌𝗍𝗈d×d\mathbf{K}\in\mathbb{R}_{\mathsf{sto}}^{d\times d} whose entries [𝐊]i,j[\mathbf{K}]_{i,j} denote the probability of transitioning from state ii to state jj (which, by homogeneity, is the same at any time). We assume that norms operate on row vectors analogously to their usual behavior on column vectors.

Below, we present an overview of pertinent results on Markov chain convergence from the literature and add new results discussing how Doeblin curves relate to these existing characterizations.

Proposition 14 (Markov Chain Properties).

Given a discrete-time finite-state time-homogeneous Markov chain represented as a row stochastic matrix 𝐊∈ℝ𝗌𝗍𝗈d×d\mathbf{K}\in\mathbb{R}_{\mathsf{sto}}^{d\times d}, the following statements are equivalent:

  1. 1.

    (Positive spectral gap [83]) |λ2​(𝐊)|<1|\lambda_{2}(\mathbf{K})|<1.

  2. 2.

    (Aperiodic unichain [83]) The Markov chain represented by 𝐊\mathbf{K} has exactly one recurrent class, and its recurrent class is aperiodic.

  3. 3.

    (Strong ergodicity [83, 84]) The Markov chain represented by 𝐊\mathbf{K} converges to a fixed steady-state distribution 𝝅∗∈𝒫d−1\boldsymbol{\pi}^{*}\in\mathscr{P}_{d-1} regardless of the initial distribution, i.e., limn→∞𝝅0​𝐊n=𝝅∗\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\boldsymbol{\pi}_{0}\mathbf{K}^{n}=\boldsymbol{\pi}^{*} for all 𝝅0∈𝒫d−1\boldsymbol{\pi}_{0}\in\mathscr{P}_{d-1}. Furthermore, the convergence is exponentially fast, i.e., there exist constants C>0C>0 and 0<α<10<\alpha<1 independent of 𝝅0\boldsymbol{\pi}_{0} such that ∥𝝅0​𝐊n−𝝅∗∥1≤C​αn\lVert\boldsymbol{\pi}_{0}\mathbf{K}^{n}-\boldsymbol{\pi}^{*}\rVert_{1}\leq C\alpha^{n} for all n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}.

  4. 4.

    (Weak ergodicity [84, 85]) The rows of 𝐊n\mathbf{K}^{n} equalize as time n→∞n\rightarrow\infty, i.e., limn→∞∥[𝐊n]⟨i⟩−[𝐊n]⟨j⟩∥∞=0\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\lVert[\mathbf{K}^{n}]_{\left\langle i\right\rangle}-[\mathbf{K}^{n}]_{\left\langle j\right\rangle}\rVert_{\infty}=0 for all i,j∈[d]i,j\in[d].

  5. 5.

    (Doeblin characterization of weak ergodicity) For all n≥d2n\geq d^{2}, τ⁡(𝐊n)>0\tau(\mathbf{K}^{n})>0.

  6. 6.

    (Doeblin curves) F𝐊n​(t,ℝ𝗌𝗍𝗈d×d)<t\mathrm{F}_{\mathbf{K}^{n}}(t;\mathbb{R}_{\mathsf{sto}}^{d\times d})<t for all n≥d2n\geq d^{2} and t∈(0,1]t\in(0,1].

Proof.

The equivalences a) through f) hold because:

  • •

    b) ⟹\implies a) by [83, Theorem 4.4.2]

  • •

    ¬\lnot\,b) ⟹⁣¬\implies\lnot\,a) by [83, Section 4.4.2, p. 178]

  • •

    b) ⟹\implies c) by [83, Theorem 4.3.7]

  • •

    ¬\lnot\,b) ⟹⁣¬\implies\lnot\,c) by [83, Section 4.3.5, p. 175]

  • •

    c) ⇔\iff d) by [84, p. 867]

  • •

    e) ⟹\implies d) by [28, Eq. 6] or [85, Theorem 4.8]

By [85, Theorem 4.8], d) implies that there exists some N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N} such that τ⁡(𝐊N)>0\tau(\mathbf{K}^{N})>0; this is a weaker version of e) that lacks an explicit dd-dependent threshold on NN. To remedy this, we supply a proof of the threshold below.

Proof of b) ⟹\implies e): Let r∈[d]r\in[d] be the number of states in the recurrent class of 𝐊\mathbf{K}, and d−rd-r the number of transient states. In the graph representation of 𝐊\mathbf{K}, for each transient state ii (if one exists), there must exist a path from ii to any state in the recurrent class of length at most d−rd-r. Fix an arbitrary state kk in the recurrent class. Since the recurrent class is aperiodic, Wielandt’s result for primitive matrices [86, Corollary 8.5.8] implies that given an arbitrary integer N≥r2−2​r+2N\geq r^{2}-2r+2, there must exist a path of length exactly NN from each recurrent state to kk. Thus, for every state ii (either transient or recurrent), there must exist a path from ii to kk of length exactly r2−3​r+d+2r^{2}-3r+d+2, which implies that τ⁡(𝐊n)>0\tau(\mathbf{K}^{n})>0 for all

n≥d2≥r2−3​r+d+2,n\geq d^{2}\geq r^{2}-3r+d+2, (624)

which holds for all d≥r≥1d\geq r\geq 1 since d2−d=d⁡(d−1)≥(r−1)​(r−2)=r2−3​r+2d^{2}-d=d(d-1)\geq(r-1)(r-2)=r^{2}-3r+2, as desired.

Although c) ⇔\iff d) is known in the literature [84, p. 867], this equivalence is seldom directly argued for homogeneous Markov chains, since the distinction between strong and weak forms of ergodicity is traditionally only made in the context of inhomogeneous chains. So, for completeness, we provide a proof of c) ⇔\iff d) from first principles below.

Proof of c) ⇔\iff d): Fix a time-homogeneous Markov chain 𝐊∈ℝ𝗌𝗍𝗈d×d\mathbf{K}\in\mathbb{R}_{\mathsf{sto}}^{d\times d}. First, we will prove the forward direction; the argument is straightforward and standard. Assume 𝐊\mathbf{K} is strongly ergodic, with 𝝅∗\boldsymbol{\pi}^{*} denoting its steady-state distribution. Then, for any i,j∈[d]i,j\in[d],

limn→∞‖[𝐊n]⟨i⟩−[𝐊n]⟨j⟩‖∞=limn→∞‖𝐞i​𝐊n−𝐞j​𝐊n‖∞\displaystyle\phantom{{}={}}\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\left\lVert\left[\mathbf{K}^{n}\right]_{\left\langle i\right\rangle}-\left[\mathbf{K}^{n}\right]_{\left\langle j\right\rangle}\right\rVert_{\infty}=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\left\lVert\mathbf{e}_{i}\mathbf{K}^{n}-\mathbf{e}_{j}\mathbf{K}^{n}\right\rVert_{\infty} (625)
≤(a)limn→∞‖𝐞i​𝐊n−𝝅∗‖∞+limn→∞‖𝐞j​𝐊n−𝝅∗‖∞=(b)0,\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(a)}}}{{\leq}}\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\left\lVert\mathbf{e}_{i}\mathbf{K}^{n}-\boldsymbol{\pi}^{*}\right\rVert_{\infty}+\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\left\lVert\mathbf{e}_{j}\mathbf{K}^{n}-\boldsymbol{\pi}^{*}\right\rVert_{\infty}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(b)}}}{{=}}0, (626)

where (a) holds by the triangle inequality and additivity of limits, and (b) holds by strong ergodicity. Hence, 𝐊\mathbf{K} is weakly ergodic, as desired.

Next, we will prove the reverse direction. Assume 𝐊\mathbf{K} is weakly ergodic. Consider the sequence of powers {𝐊n}n=1∞\{\mathbf{K}^{n}\}_{n=1}^{\infty}. Since the set of all row stochastic matrices ℝ𝗌𝗍𝗈d×d\mathbb{R}_{\mathsf{sto}}^{d\times d} is compact (e.g., under the Frobenius norm), there exists a subsequence {𝐊nℓ}ℓ=1∞\{\mathbf{K}^{n_{\ell}}\}_{\ell=1}^{\infty} which converges to a limit 𝐊∗∈ℝ𝗌𝗍𝗈d×d\mathbf{K}^{*}\in\mathbb{R}_{\mathsf{sto}}^{d\times d}, i.e.,

limℓ→∞‖𝐊nℓ−𝐊∗‖F=0.\lim_{\ell\rightarrow\infty}\left\lVert\mathbf{K}^{n_{\ell}}-\mathbf{K}^{*}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}=0. (627)

Furthermore, for any i,j∈[d]i,j\in[d], we have

‖[𝐊∗]⟨i⟩−[𝐊∗]⟨j⟩‖∞\displaystyle\phantom{{}={}}\left\lVert\left[\mathbf{K}^{*}\right]_{\left\langle i\right\rangle}-\left[\mathbf{K}^{*}\right]_{\left\langle j\right\rangle}\right\rVert_{\infty} (628)
≤(a)limℓ→∞‖[𝐊nℓ]⟨i⟩−[𝐊∗]⟨i⟩‖∞+limℓ→∞‖[𝐊nℓ]⟨j⟩−[𝐊∗]⟨j⟩‖∞\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(a)}}}{{\leq}}\lim_{\ell\rightarrow\infty}\left\lVert\left[\mathbf{K}^{n_{\ell}}\right]_{\left\langle i\right\rangle}-\left[\mathbf{K}^{*}\right]_{\left\langle i\right\rangle}\right\rVert_{\infty}\!\!\!+\lim_{\ell\rightarrow\infty}\left\lVert\left[\mathbf{K}^{n_{\ell}}\right]_{\left\langle j\right\rangle}-\left[\mathbf{K}^{*}\right]_{\left\langle j\right\rangle}\right\rVert_{\infty} (629)
+limℓ→∞‖[𝐊nℓ]⟨i⟩−[𝐊nℓ]⟨j⟩‖∞\displaystyle\phantom{{}={}}+\lim_{\ell\rightarrow\infty}\left\lVert\left[\mathbf{K}^{n_{\ell}}\right]_{\left\langle i\right\rangle}-\left[\mathbf{K}^{n_{\ell}}\right]_{\left\langle j\right\rangle}\right\rVert_{\infty} (630)
=(b)limℓ→∞‖[𝐊nℓ]⟨i⟩−[𝐊nℓ]⟨j⟩‖∞\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(b)}}}{{=}}\lim_{\ell\rightarrow\infty}\left\lVert\left[\mathbf{K}^{n_{\ell}}\right]_{\left\langle i\right\rangle}-\left[\mathbf{K}^{n_{\ell}}\right]_{\left\langle j\right\rangle}\right\rVert_{\infty} (631)
=(c)limn→∞‖[𝐊n]⟨i⟩−[𝐊n]⟨j⟩‖∞=(d)0,\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(c)}}}{{=}}\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\left\lVert\left[\mathbf{K}^{n}\right]_{\left\langle i\right\rangle}-\left[\mathbf{K}^{n}\right]_{\left\langle j\right\rangle}\right\rVert_{\infty}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(d)}}}{{=}}0, (632)

where (a) holds by the triangle inequality and additivity of limits, (b) holds by Equation 627, (c) holds because the limit of any subsequence of a convergent sequence is equal to the limit of the entire sequence, and (d) holds by weak ergodicity. Hence, 𝐊∗\mathbf{K}^{*} has all identical rows, and so rank⁡(𝐊∗)=1\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{K}^{*})=1. Therefore, |λ1​(𝐊∗)|>0\lvert\lambda_{1}(\mathbf{K}^{*})\rvert>0 and λ2​(𝐊∗)=⋅⋅⋅=λd​(𝐊∗)=0\lambda_{2}(\mathbf{K}^{*})=\mathinner{\cdotp\mkern-2.0mu\cdotp\mkern-2.0mu\cdotp}=\lambda_{d}(\mathbf{K}^{*})=0.

Moreover, by the Perron-Frobenius theorem [85, Chapter 1], we have λ1​(𝐊∗)=1\lambda_{1}(\mathbf{K}^{*})=1 and λ1​(𝐊n)=1\lambda_{1}(\mathbf{K}^{n})=1 for every n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}. For any initial distribution 𝝅0=𝐜𝐗∈𝒫d−1\boldsymbol{\pi}_{0}=\mathbf{c}\mathbf{X}\in\mathscr{P}_{d-1}, we have

limn→∞𝝅0​𝐊n\displaystyle\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\boldsymbol{\pi}_{0}\mathbf{K}^{n} =limn→∞{(𝐜𝐗)​(𝐗−1​𝐉n​𝐗)}=𝐜⁡(limn→∞𝐉n)​𝐗\displaystyle=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\left\{\left(\mathbf{c}\mathbf{X}\right)\left(\mathbf{X}^{-1}\mathbf{J}^{n}\mathbf{X}\right)\right\}=\mathbf{c}\left(\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\mathbf{J}^{n}\right)\mathbf{X} (633)
=(a)𝐜𝐞1T​𝐞1​𝐗=[𝐜]1​[𝐗]⟨1⟩,\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(a)}}}{{=}}\mathbf{c}\mathbf{e}_{1}^{\mathrm{T}}\mathbf{e}_{1}\mathbf{X}=\left[\mathbf{c}\right]_{1}\left[\mathbf{X}\right]_{\left\langle 1\right\rangle}, (634)

where (a) holds because the powers of Jordan blocks corresponding to eigenvalues with magnitude less than 11 vanish entry-wise in the limit. Proof of e) ⇔\iff f): The set of all d×dd\times d row stochastic matrices ℝ𝗌𝗍𝗈d×d\mathbb{R}_{\mathsf{sto}}^{d\times d} is convex, contains the identity kernel (i.e., the d×dd\times d identity matrix), and contains a constant kernel (e.g., the d×dd\times d matrix where each row is 𝐞1\mathbf{e}_{1}). Thus, by Proposition 3, Part 2,

F𝐊n​(t,ℝ𝗌𝗍𝗈d×d)=ρ⁡(𝐊n)​t.\displaystyle\mathrm{F}_{\mathbf{K}^{n}}\left(t;\mathbb{R}_{\mathsf{sto}}^{d\times d}\right)=\rho\left(\mathbf{K}^{n}\right)\,t. (635)

Hence, F𝐊n​(t,ℝ𝗌𝗍𝗈d×d)<t\mathrm{F}_{\mathbf{K}^{n}}(t;\mathbb{R}_{\mathsf{sto}}^{d\times d})<t holds iff ρ⁡(𝐊n)<1\rho(\mathbf{K}^{n})<1, or equivalently τ⁡(𝐊n)>0\tau(\mathbf{K}^{n})>0, as desired. ∎

Proposition 14 states that any Markov chain 𝐊∈ℝ𝗌𝗍𝗈d×d\mathbf{K}\in\mathbb{R}_{\mathsf{sto}}^{d\times d} has positive spectral gap (i.e., |λ2​(𝐊)|<1|\lambda_{2}(\mathbf{K})|<1) iff F𝐊n​(t,ℝ𝗌𝗍𝗈d×d)<t\mathrm{F}_{\mathbf{K}^{n}}(t;\mathbb{R}_{\mathsf{sto}}^{d\times d})<t holds for sufficiently large nn. We note that taking into account whether the inequality holds for sufficiently high power 𝐊n\mathbf{K}^{n}, not necessarily 𝐊\mathbf{K} itself, is crucial to this equivalence, as |λ2​(𝐊)|<1|\lambda_{2}(\mathbf{K})|<1 does not imply in general that the inequality holds for n=1n=1. As a counterexample, consider a directed cycle on d≥4d\geq 4 vertices with self-loops at each vertex:

∀i,j∈[d],[𝐊]i,j={12,if j=i,12,if j=i+1 or (i,j)=(d,1),0,otherwise.\forall i,j\in[d],\quad\left[\mathbf{K}\right]_{i,j}=\!\begin{cases}\frac{1}{2},&\text{if $j=i$},\\ \frac{1}{2},&\text{if $j=i+1$ or $(i,j)=(d,1)$},\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (636)

Clearly, 𝐊\mathbf{K} has positive spectral gap because it is a unichain (by virtue of its cycle structure) and aperiodic (by virtue of its self-loops). Now, let 𝐰\mathbf{w} and 𝐯\mathbf{v} be point mass distributions at vertices at least distance 22 apart on the cycle, e.g., 𝐰=𝐞1\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{e}_{1} and 𝐯=𝐞3\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{e}_{3}. Then, by matrix multiplication, the distributions after one step of 𝐊\mathbf{K} are 𝐰𝐊=(1/2)​𝐞1+(1/2)​𝐞2\mathbf{w}\mathbf{K}=(1/2)\mathbf{e}_{1}+(1/2)\mathbf{e}_{2} and 𝐯𝐊=(1/2)​𝐞3+(1/2)​𝐞4.\mathbf{v}\mathbf{K}=(1/2)\mathbf{e}_{3}+(1/2)\mathbf{e}_{4}. It follows that

ρ⁡(𝐊)=(a)ρ⁡([𝐰,𝐯])​ρ​(𝐊)≥(b)ρ⁡([𝐰𝐊,𝐯𝐊])=(c)1,\rho(\mathbf{K})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(a)}}}{{=}}\rho\bigl(\left[\mathbf{w},\mathbf{v}\right]\bigr)\,\rho(\mathbf{K})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(b)}}}{{\geq}}\rho\bigl(\left[\mathbf{w}\mathbf{K},\mathbf{v}\mathbf{K}\right]\bigr)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(c)}}}{{=}}1, (637)

where (a) holds because 𝐰=𝐞1\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{e}_{1} and 𝐯=𝐞3\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{e}_{3} have disjoint support and thus ρ⁡([𝐰,𝐯])=1\rho([\mathbf{w},\mathbf{v}])=1, (b) holds by submultiplicativity of complementary Doeblin coefficients, and (c) holds because 𝐰𝐊\mathbf{w}\mathbf{K} and 𝐯𝐊\mathbf{v}\mathbf{K} have disjoint support. By Equation 635, it follows that F𝐊​(t,ℝ𝗌𝗍𝗈d×d)=t\mathrm{F}_{\mathbf{K}}(t;\mathbb{R}_{\mathsf{sto}}^{d\times d})=t, even though 𝐊\mathbf{K} has positive spectral gap.

Next, we present the following proposition which exactly characterizes when contraction occurs between two input distributions after one step of the Markov chain 𝐊\mathbf{K}.2121 21 Since we consider two input distributions, the Doeblin coefficient ρ\rho reduces to TV distance.

Proposition 15 (Strict Contraction of Doeblin Coefficient).

Let 𝐊∈ℝ𝗌𝗍𝗈d×d\mathbf{K}\in\mathbb{R}_{\mathsf{sto}}^{d\times d} be a Markov chain. For any subset of states 𝒮⊆[d]\mathcal{S}\subseteq[d], let 𝒩𝐊​(𝒮)\mathcal{N}_{\mathbf{K}}(\mathcal{S}) denote the set of states reachable from 𝒮\mathcal{S} in one time step, i.e.,

𝒩𝐊(𝒮)={j∈[d]:∃i∈[d],[𝐊]i,j>0}.\mathcal{N}_{\mathbf{K}}(\mathcal{S})=\left\{j\in[d]:\exists i\in[d],\,\left[\mathbf{K}\right]_{i,j}>0\right\}. (638)

Then, for any pair of distributions 𝐰,𝐯∈𝒫d−1\mathbf{w},\mathbf{v}\in\mathscr{P}_{d-1}, we have ρ⁡([𝐰,𝐯]​𝐊)<ρ⁡([𝐰,𝐯])\rho(\left[\mathbf{w},\mathbf{v}\right]\mathbf{K})<\rho(\left[\mathbf{w},\mathbf{v}\right]) iff 𝒩𝐊​(𝒮𝐰>𝐯)∩𝒩𝐊​(𝒮𝐰<𝐯)\mathcal{N}_{\mathbf{K}}(\mathcal{S}_{\mathbf{w}>\mathbf{v}})\cap\mathcal{N}_{\mathbf{K}}(\mathcal{S}_{\mathbf{w}<\mathbf{v}}) is non-empty, where we define

𝒮𝐰>𝐯\displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{\mathbf{w}>\mathbf{v}} ={i∈[d]:[𝐰]i>[𝐯]i},\displaystyle=\left\{i\in[d]:\left[\mathbf{w}\right]_{i}>\left[\mathbf{v}\right]_{i}\right\}, (639)
𝒮𝐰<𝐯\displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{\mathbf{w}<\mathbf{v}} ={i∈[d]:[𝐰]i<[𝐯]i}.\displaystyle=\left\{i\in[d]:\left[\mathbf{w}\right]_{i}<\left[\mathbf{v}\right]_{i}\right\}. (640)
Proof.

Fix a Markov chain 𝐊∈ℝ𝗌𝗍𝗈d×d\mathbf{K}\in\mathbb{R}_{\mathsf{sto}}^{d\times d} and distributions 𝐰,𝐯∈𝒫d−1\mathbf{w},\mathbf{v}\in\mathscr{P}_{d-1}. We have

ρ⁡([𝐰,𝐯]​𝐊)\displaystyle\rho\bigl(\left[\mathbf{w},\mathbf{v}\right]\mathbf{K}\bigr) =(a)1−∑j=1dmin⁡{[𝐰𝐊]j,[𝐯𝐊]j}\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(a)}}}{{=}}1-\sum_{j=1}^{d}\min\left\{\left[\mathbf{w}\mathbf{K}\right]_{j},\left[\mathbf{v}\mathbf{K}\right]_{j}\right\} (641)
=(b)1−∑j=1dmin⁡{∑i=1d[𝐰]i​[𝐊]i,j,∑i=1d[𝐯]i​[𝐊]i,j}\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(b)}}}{{=}}1-\sum_{j=1}^{d}\min\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{d}\left[\mathbf{w}\right]_{i}\left[\mathbf{K}\right]_{i,j},\sum_{i=1}^{d}\left[\mathbf{v}\right]_{i}\left[\mathbf{K}\right]_{i,j}\right\} (642)
≤(c)1−∑j=1d∑i=1dmin⁡{[𝐰]i​[𝐊]i,j,[𝐯]i​[𝐊]i,j}\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(c)}}}{{\leq}}1-\sum_{j=1}^{d}\sum_{i=1}^{d}\min\left\{\left[\mathbf{w}\right]_{i}\left[\mathbf{K}\right]_{i,j},\left[\mathbf{v}\right]_{i}\left[\mathbf{K}\right]_{i,j}\right\} (643)
=(d)1−∑i=1dmin⁡{[𝐰]i,[𝐯]i}​∑j=1d[𝐊]i,j\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(d)}}}{{=}}1-\sum_{i=1}^{d}\min\left\{\left[\mathbf{w}\right]_{i},\left[\mathbf{v}\right]_{i}\right\}\sum_{j=1}^{d}\left[\mathbf{K}\right]_{i,j} (644)
=(e)1−∑i=1dmin⁡{[𝐰]i,[𝐯]i}\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(e)}}}{{=}}1-\sum_{i=1}^{d}\min\left\{\left[\mathbf{w}\right]_{i},\left[\mathbf{v}\right]_{i}\right\} (645)
=(f)ρ⁡([𝐰,𝐯]),\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(f)}}}{{=}}\rho\bigl(\left[\mathbf{w},\mathbf{v}\right]\bigr), (646)

where (a) holds by definition of Doeblin coefficient Equation 12, (b) holds by matrix algebra, (c) holds by the identity

min⁡{∑ixi,∑iyi}≥∑imin⁡{xi,yi},\min\left\{\sum_{i}x_{i},\sum_{i}y_{i}\right\}\geq\sum_{i}\min\left\{x_{i},y_{i}\right\}, (647)

(d) holds by factoring [𝐊]i,j[\mathbf{K}]_{i,j} outside the minimum (because [𝐊]i,j≥0[\mathbf{K}]_{i,j}\geq 0) and interchanging the order of summation, (e) holds because 𝐊\mathbf{K} is row stochastic, and (f) holds by definition of Doeblin coefficient Equation 12. The inequality in Equation 647 is strict iff xi>yix_{i}>y_{i} and xi′<yi′x_{i^{\prime}}<y_{i^{\prime}} for some ii and i′i^{\prime}. Hence, the inequality in step (c) of Equation 646 is strict iff there exist i,i′,j∈[d]i,i^{\prime},j\in[d] such that [𝐰]i>[𝐯]i\left[\mathbf{w}\right]_{i}>\left[\mathbf{v}\right]_{i} and [𝐊]i,j>0\left[\mathbf{K}\right]_{i,j}>0 (i.e., j∈𝒩𝐊​(𝒮𝐰>𝐯)j\in\mathcal{N}_{\mathbf{K}}(\mathcal{S}_{\mathbf{w}>\mathbf{v}})), and [𝐰]i′<[𝐯]i′\left[\mathbf{w}\right]_{i^{\prime}}<\left[\mathbf{v}\right]_{i^{\prime}} and [𝐊]i′,j>0\left[\mathbf{K}\right]_{i^{\prime},j}>0 (i.e., j∈𝒩𝐊​(𝒮𝐰<𝐯)j\in\mathcal{N}_{\mathbf{K}}(\mathcal{S}_{\mathbf{w}<\mathbf{v}})).2222 22 This condition for equality can also be verified by using the ℓ1\ell^{1}-norm characterization of TV distance in (a), applying the triangle inequality to deduce (e), and then using known conditions for equality in the triangle inequality. Clearly, this is equivalent to the condition that 𝒩𝐊​(𝒮𝐰>𝐯)∩𝒩𝐊​(𝒮𝐰<𝐯)≠∅\mathcal{N}_{\mathbf{K}}(\mathcal{S}_{\mathbf{w}>\mathbf{v}})\cap\mathcal{N}_{\mathbf{K}}(\mathcal{S}_{\mathbf{w}<\mathbf{v}})\neq\emptyset, as desired. ∎

Proposition 15 exactly characterizes the condition on 𝐊\mathbf{K}, 𝐰\mathbf{w}, 𝐯\mathbf{v} such that strict contraction occurs in one step. We remark that two natural corollaries of this result give intuitive conditions on 𝐊\mathbf{K} under which strict contraction occurs for entire classes of 𝐰\mathbf{w} and 𝐯\mathbf{v}.

Corollary 3 (Strict Contraction and Gramian).

Let 𝐊∈ℝ𝗌𝗍𝗈d×d\mathbf{K}\in\mathbb{R}_{\mathsf{sto}}^{d\times d} be a Markov chain. The joint range of 𝐊\mathbf{K} satisfies 𝔉⁡(𝐊,ℝ𝗌𝗍𝗈2×d)⊆{(t,y)∈[0,1]2:y<t}∪{(0,0)}\mathfrak{F}(\mathbf{K};\mathbb{R}_{\mathsf{sto}}^{2\times d})\subseteq\{(t,y)\in[0,1]^{2}:y<t\}\cup\{(0,0)\}, or, equivalently, we have ρ⁡([𝐰,𝐯]​𝐊)<ρ⁡([𝐰,𝐯])\rho([\mathbf{w},\mathbf{v}]\mathbf{K})<\rho([\mathbf{w},\mathbf{v}]) for all pairs of distinct distributions 𝐰,𝐯∈𝒫d−1\mathbf{w},\mathbf{v}\in\mathscr{P}_{d-1}, iff the Gramian matrix 𝐊𝐊T\mathbf{K}\mathbf{K}^{\mathrm{T}} is entry-wise strictly positive.

Proof.

Fix 𝐊∈ℝ𝗌𝗍𝗈d×d\mathbf{K}\in\mathbb{R}_{\mathsf{sto}}^{d\times d}.

First, we will prove the forward direction. Assume 𝐊𝐊T\mathbf{K}\mathbf{K}^{\mathrm{T}} is entry-wise strictly positive. Fix any distinct distributions 𝐰,𝐯∈𝒫d−1\mathbf{w},\mathbf{v}\in\mathscr{P}_{d-1}. Recall the definitions of 𝒮𝐰>𝐯\mathcal{S}_{\mathbf{w}>\mathbf{v}} and 𝒮𝐰<𝐯\mathcal{S}_{\mathbf{w}<\mathbf{v}} from Equation 640. Since probability distributions sum to 11, both 𝒮𝐰>𝐯\mathcal{S}_{\mathbf{w}>\mathbf{v}} and 𝒮𝐰<𝐯\mathcal{S}_{\mathbf{w}<\mathbf{v}} are non-empty. Consider any i∈𝒮𝐰>𝐯i\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathbf{w}>\mathbf{v}} and i′∈𝒮𝐯<𝐰i^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathbf{v}<\mathbf{w}}. By assumption, we have [𝐊𝐊T]i,i′=∑j=1d[𝐊]i,j​[𝐊]i′,j>0,[\mathbf{K}\mathbf{K}^{\mathrm{T}}]_{i,i^{\prime}}=\sum_{j=1}^{d}[\mathbf{K}]_{i,j}[\mathbf{K}]_{i^{\prime},j}>0, so there exists j∗∈[d]j^{*}\in[d] such that [𝐊]i,j∗>0[\mathbf{K}]_{i,j^{*}}>0 and [𝐊]i′,j∗>0[\mathbf{K}]_{i^{\prime},j^{*}}>0. By Equation 638, it holds that j∗∈𝒩𝐊​(𝒮𝐰>𝐯)j^{*}\in\mathcal{N}_{\mathbf{K}}(\mathcal{S}_{\mathbf{w}>\mathbf{v}}) and j∗∈𝒩𝐊​(𝒮𝐰<𝐯)j^{*}\in\mathcal{N}_{\mathbf{K}}(\mathcal{S}_{\mathbf{w}<\mathbf{v}}), and so 𝒩𝐊​(𝒮𝐰>𝐯)∩𝒩𝐊​(𝒮𝐰<𝐯)≠∅\mathcal{N}_{\mathbf{K}}(\mathcal{S}_{\mathbf{w}>\mathbf{v}})\cap\mathcal{N}_{\mathbf{K}}(\mathcal{S}_{\mathbf{w}<\mathbf{v}})\neq\emptyset. By Proposition 15, we have ρ⁡([𝐰,𝐯]​𝐊)<ρ⁡([𝐰,𝐯])\rho([\mathbf{w},\mathbf{v}]\,\mathbf{K})<\rho([\mathbf{w},\mathbf{v}]) as desired.

Next, we will prove the reverse direction. Assume that ρ⁡([𝐰,𝐯]​𝐊)<ρ⁡([𝐰,𝐯])\rho([\mathbf{w},\mathbf{v}]\,\mathbf{K})<\rho([\mathbf{w},\mathbf{v}]) for any distinct distributions 𝐰,𝐯∈𝒫d−1\mathbf{w},\mathbf{v}\in\mathscr{P}_{d-1}. Fix unspecified distinct i,i′∈[d]i,i^{\prime}\in[d]. Choosing 𝐰=𝐞i\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{e}_{i} and 𝐯=𝐞i′\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{e}_{i^{\prime}} and applying Proposition 15, we have 𝒩𝐊​({i})∩𝒩𝐊​({i′})≠∅\mathcal{N}_{\mathbf{K}}(\left\{i\right\})\cap\mathcal{N}_{\mathbf{K}}(\{i^{\prime}\})\neq\emptyset. Consider any j∗∈𝒩𝐊​({i})∩𝒩𝐊​({i′})j^{*}\in\mathcal{N}_{\mathbf{K}}(\{i\})\cap\mathcal{N}_{\mathbf{K}}(\{i^{\prime}\}). We have

[𝐊𝐊T]i,i′=∑j=1d[𝐊]i,j​[𝐊]i′,j≥[𝐊]i,j∗​[𝐊]i′,j∗>(a)0,\left[\mathbf{K}\mathbf{K}^{\mathrm{T}}\right]_{i,i^{\prime}}=\sum_{j=1}^{d}\left[\mathbf{K}\right]_{i,j}\left[\mathbf{K}\right]_{i^{\prime},j}\geq\left[\mathbf{K}\right]_{i,j^{*}}\left[\mathbf{K}\right]_{i^{\prime},j^{*}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathclap{(a)}}}{{>}}0, (648)

where (a) holds by definition of 𝒩𝐊\mathcal{N}_{\mathbf{K}} from Equation 638, and so the off-diagonal entries of 𝐊𝐊T\mathbf{K}\mathbf{K}^{\mathrm{T}} are positive. Furthermore, for any i∈[d]i\in[d], we have [𝐊𝐊T]i,i=∑j=1d[𝐊]i,j2>0,[\mathbf{K}\mathbf{K}^{\mathrm{T}}]_{i,i}=\sum_{j=1}^{d}[\mathbf{K}]_{i,j}^{2}>0, where the final inequality holds because 𝐊\mathbf{K} is row stochastic, and so the diagonal entries of 𝐊𝐊T\mathbf{K}\mathbf{K}^{\mathrm{T}} are positive. Hence, 𝐊𝐊T\mathbf{K}\mathbf{K}^{\mathrm{T}} is entry-wise strictly positive, as desired. ∎

Corollary 4 (Strict Contraction and Laziness).

Let 𝐊∈ℝ𝗌𝗍𝗈d×d\mathbf{K}\in\mathbb{R}_{\mathsf{sto}}^{d\times d} be a lazy Markov chain (i.e., [𝐊]i,i>0[\mathbf{K}]_{i,i}>0 for all i∈[d]i\in[d]) with positive spectral gap (i.e., |λ2​(𝐊)|<1|\lambda_{2}(\mathbf{K})|<1). Then, for all pairs of distributions 𝐰,𝐯∈𝒫d−1\mathbf{w},\mathbf{v}\in\mathscr{P}_{d-1} which differ at each entry (i.e., [𝐰]i≠[𝐯]i[\mathbf{w}]_{i}\neq[\mathbf{v}]_{i} for all i∈[d]i\in[d]), we have ρ⁡([𝐰,𝐯]​𝐊)<ρ⁡([𝐰,𝐯])\rho([\mathbf{w},\mathbf{v}]\mathbf{K})<\rho([\mathbf{w},\mathbf{v}]).

Proof.

Fix a Markov chain 𝐊∈ℝ𝗌𝗍𝗈d×d\mathbf{K}\in\mathbb{R}_{\mathsf{sto}}^{d\times d} and distributions 𝐰,𝐯∈𝒫d−1\mathbf{w},\mathbf{v}\in\mathscr{P}_{d-1} satisfying the conditions in Corollary 4. Since 𝐰\mathbf{w} and 𝐯\mathbf{v} differ at each entry, we have 𝒮𝐰>𝐯c=𝒮𝐰<𝐯\mathcal{S}_{\mathbf{w}>\mathbf{v}}^{\mathrm{c}}=\mathcal{S}_{\mathbf{w}<\mathbf{v}}. Since 𝐊\mathbf{K} has positive spectral gap, 𝐊\mathbf{K} has exactly one recurrent class (by Proposition 14, Part (b)), and so the directed graph representation of 𝐊\mathbf{K} is connected (in an undirected sense). Hence, there exists an edge between 𝒮𝐰>𝐯\mathcal{S}_{\mathbf{w}>\mathbf{v}} and 𝒮𝐰>𝐯c\mathcal{S}_{\mathbf{w}>\mathbf{v}}^{\mathrm{c}}, i.e., for some i∈𝒮𝐰>𝐯i\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathbf{w}>\mathbf{v}} and i′∈𝒮𝐰<𝐯i^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathbf{w}<\mathbf{v}}, we have [𝐊]i,i′>0[\mathbf{K}]_{i,i^{\prime}}>0 or [𝐊]i′,i>0[\mathbf{K}]_{i^{\prime},i}>0. Without loss of generality, assume [𝐊]i,i′>0[\mathbf{K}]_{i,i^{\prime}}>0. Since 𝐊\mathbf{K} is lazy, we have [𝐊]i′,i′>0[\mathbf{K}]_{i^{\prime},i^{\prime}}>0. By Equation 638, it holds that i′∈𝒩𝐊​(𝒮𝐰>𝐯)i^{\prime}\in\mathcal{N}_{\mathbf{K}}(\mathcal{S}_{\mathbf{w}>\mathbf{v}}) and i′∈𝒩𝐊​(𝒮𝐰<𝐯)i^{\prime}\in\mathcal{N}_{\mathbf{K}}(\mathcal{S}_{\mathbf{w}<\mathbf{v}}), and so 𝒩𝐊​(𝒮𝐰>𝐯)∩𝒩𝐊​(𝒮𝐰<𝐯)≠∅\mathcal{N}_{\mathbf{K}}(\mathcal{S}_{\mathbf{w}>\mathbf{v}})\cap\mathcal{N}_{\mathbf{K}}(\mathcal{S}_{\mathbf{w}<\mathbf{v}})\neq\emptyset. By Proposition 15, we have ρ⁡([𝐰,𝐯]​𝐊)<ρ⁡([𝐰,𝐯])\rho([\mathbf{w},\mathbf{v}]\,\mathbf{K})<\rho([\mathbf{w},\mathbf{v}]) as desired. ∎

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
